title: Computerized fine motor assessment in Parkinson's Disease: Task-specific measures provide complementary clinical information.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Fine motor impairment is a common feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) and contributes substantially to functional disability. Although the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS Part III) remains the standard clinical tool for motor evaluation, quantitative computerized assessments may provide complementary task-specific information. OBJECTIVES: This cross-sectional case-control study compared fine motor performance measured using the Motorische Leistungs-Serie (MLS) between 19 patients with idiopathic PD and 20 healthy controls and examined associations between MLS-derived parameters and clinical motor severity. METHODS: Motor performance was evaluated using five MLS subtests covering aiming behavior, hand steadiness, precision arm-hand coordination, speed arm-hand, and speed wrist-finger tasks. RESULTS: After adjustment for age, sex, and educational level, patients with PD showed significantly poorer overall fine motor performance, as reflected by the Composite Motor Performance Score, together with significant impairments in selected task-specific measures of aiming performance and visuomotor tracking. Several MLS-derived parameters, particularly aiming duration and hand steadiness, were significantly associated with MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that MLS-derived task-specific measures provide objective quantitative information that complements conventional clinical motor assessment in Parkinson's disease. Analysis of individual task-specific parameters may provide complementary clinically relevant information beyond a single global composite score. However, larger prospective studies are required to determine the clinical utility of task-specific computerized fine motor assessment for monitoring disease progression and treatment response.

title: A contactless approach for accurate sleep stage detection using the Sleepal AI Lamp.
abstract: Objective.To validate the accuracy and clinical feasibility of a noncontact radar system (Sleepal AI Lamp) for assessing sleep architecture and staging. Although noncontact radar sensors can capture respiratory and motor mechanics without physical attachment, robust validation in large-scale, pathologically diverse cohorts remains scarce.Approach.Nocturnal respiratory and body movement signals were assessed in 1022 adults using simultaneous measurements from a frequency-modulated continuous-wave bedside radar and gold-standard Polysomnography. The cohort included individuals with normal sleep profiles and patients with varying severities of obstructive sleep apnea. A frequency-augmented deep learning architecture interpreted these respiratory and movement signals.Main results.In the independent validation set, binary sleep-wake classification achieved 92.7% accuracy, a Cohen's kappa of 0.792, 96.4% sleep sensitivity, 80.8% sleep specificity, and a macro-averagedF1 score of 0.896. Four-stage classification (Wake, Light, Deep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep) achieved 77.2% accuracy, a Cohen's kappa of 0.677, a macro-averagedF1 score of 0.768, and balanced accuracy/macro-recall of 77.4%, with stage-specificF1 scores of 0.839, 0.740, 0.691, and 0.802 for Wake, Light, Deep, and REM, respectively.Significance.The findings support the validity of the 60 GHz radar-based system for automated assessment of sleep macrostructure. By capturing stage-specific respiratory and movement phenotypes without physical attachment, this technology may provide an unobtrusive tool for home-based screening, longitudinal recovery tracking, and population-level sleep epidemiology.

title: Targeting the Calcium-mtDNA-cGAS-STING Signaling Nexus: A Novel Redox Mechanism for Nimodipine's Neuroprotection in Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) induces severe secondary injury where molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the involvement of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway in this process and evaluates the neuroprotective effect of the L-type calcium channel blocker nimodipine, focusing on calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory signaling. METHODS: Using primary neuronal and mouse TBI models, we assessed outcomes via fluorescent calcium imaging, JC-1 staining, Western blot, quantitative PCR (qPCR)/reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and behavioral tests. Nimodipine was applied to inhibit L-type channels, specifically testing its role in reducing mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, blocking cGAS-STING activation, and suppressing neuroinflammation. RESULTS: TBI markedly activated the cGAS-STING pathway, increasing pro-inflammatory factors and apoptosis. In the cellular oxygen-glucose deprivation model, calcium overload was directly observed by Fluo-4 AM staining and was associated with subsequent mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and mtDNA release, identifying this process as a key upstream event for cGAS-STING activation. Nimodipine inhibited intracellular calcium overload, reduced mitochondrial injury and mtDNA release, and consequently suppressed cGAS-STING pathway activation. Both in vivo and in vitro experiments showed dose-dependent decreases in pro-inflammatory factors, along with improved neurological function and attenuated brain tissue pathology. CONCLUSION: Nimodipine attenuates secondary neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis after TBI by inhibiting calcium influx, decreasing mtDNA release, and suppressing cGAS-STING signaling. These results suggest that the Ca2+-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis contributes to TBI pathology and that nimodipine may serve as a potential multitarget therapy. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.

title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-hour continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

title: cAMP signaling promotes acute lysosome biogenesis through TFEB nuclear import-export dynamics.
abstract: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling is a major stimulus for lipid and glucose catabolism, yet catabolic processes like these can also coordinate with lysosome-dependent degradation. However, the impact of cAMP signaling on lysosomal dynamics remains unclear. Transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, is regulated by stimulus-dependent nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling through a variety of phosphorylation events. Here, we find that elevating intracellular cAMP with forskolin and IBMX induces rapid nuclear import of TFEB-GFP within 30 minutes and coincides with a transient upregulation of TFEB target lysosome genes. By 8 hours, TFEB returns to the cytoplasm, accompanied by transcriptional downregulation. Inhibition of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) using H89 did not block nuclear import but unexpectedly caused sustained nuclear accumulation, indicating that PKA promotes TFEB nuclear export. Consistent with this, phosphoproteomic profiling revealed increased phosphorylation of a PKA-consensus motif (RRxS) during the export phase. These findings suggest that cAMP-PKA signaling plays a novel role in temporally "tuning" lysosomal gene expression by regulating TFEB nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling.

title: Elastin-derived peptide VGVAPG induces redox-associated pro-inflammatory activation and early disease-associated microglia (DAM) molecular profile in a human microglia-neuron in vitro model involving NEU1/TLR4-related signaling.
abstract: The elastin-derived hexapeptide Val-Gly-Val-Ala-Pro-Gly (VGVAPG) exhibits well-documented biological activity; however, its role in brain inflammation remains insufficiently characterized. This is an important issue, as VGVAPG levels increase with age and have been implicated in processes contributing to neurodegeneration. The present study aimed to evaluate the ability of aging-related VGVAPG to activate human microglial (HMC3) cells in vitro and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Our results demonstrated no cytotoxic effect of VGVAPG. However, further analyses revealed NF-κB nuclear translocation, elevated ROS and •NO production, enhanced iNOS, and accumulation of NLRP3-containing vesicles in the cytoplasm, consistent with the peptide's pro-inflammatory potential. Additionally, activation of stress- and inflammation-related signaling pathways involving p38-MAPK, JNKs, and ERK1/2 was observed, accompanied by upregulation of NFKB1, IL1B, and TNFα mRNA. Using a transwell co-culture model of HMC3 and cholinergic-like neurons (differentiated SH-SY5Y), we observed potential DAMP-associated molecular changes involving HMGB1 and APP. Additionally, NEU1 siRNA-mediated knockdown in HMC3 cells, together with the observed NEU1/TLR4 colocalization, raises the possibility that NEU1 and TLR4 may be involved in the effects induced by VGVAPG. Moreover, VGVAPG induced alterations in early disease-associated microglia (DAM)-related protein profiles, including β2M, ITGAX, and ICAM1. Collectively, these findings identify VGVAPG as a candidate pro-neuroinflammatory matrikine in vitro and provide associative evidence for selected redox, NEU1-, TLR4-related, and early DAM-associated molecular changes. Further investigations employing advanced in vivo and translational models are warranted to validate these observations and to clarify the pathophysiological role of VGVAPG in the progression of neurodegenerative disorders.

title: SIRT5 Attenuates Traumatic Brain Injury by Preserving OPA1-Mediated Mitochondrial Fusion and Limiting Oxidative Stress.
abstract: AIMS: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central pathological drivers of disease progression following traumatic brain injury (TBI). Sirtuin 5 (SIRT5), a predominantly mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacylase, plays critical roles in mitochondrial quality control, redox homeostasis, and metabolic regulation. This study aims to define the upstream regulatory machinery controlling SIRT5 stability and to identify the downstream pathway linking SIRT5 to mitochondrial remodeling after TBI. RESULTS: In this study, we demonstrated that TBI promotes neuronal SIRT5 protein degradation via a synergistic regulatory mechanism involving USP7 and TRIM21. Using neuron-specific Sirt5 conditional knockout mice, we found that SIRT5 deficiency exacerbates TBI-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative damage, cerebral edema, and neurological deficits. SIRT5 regulates OPA1 expression through a MEF2A-dependent mechanism, thereby preserving mitochondrial structure and function and alleviating oxidative injury. The protective effects of neuronal SIRT5 overexpression were abolished in mice lacking Opa1 specifically in neurons, confirming that OPA1 is a critical downstream effector of SIRT5-mediated neuroprotection. Finally, rabies virus glycoprotein (RVG)-conjugated extracellular vesicles loaded with SIRT5 mRNA demonstrated both efficacy and safety in preclinical TBI models. INNOVATION: This study identifies the USP7/TRIM21-SIRT5-MEF2A-OPA1 axis as a novel regulatory cascade that governs the transition between adaptive and maladaptive mitochondrial remodeling after TBI, a concept with broad implications for acute brain injury and neurodegeneration. CONCLUSION: This study defines the USP7/TRIM21-SIRT5-MEF2A-OPA1 axis as a novel regulatory cascade that controls mitochondrial remodeling after TBI. SIRT5 acts through a MEF2A-dependent mechanism to maintain OPA1 expression and mitochondrial fusion, and its transient restoration via RVG-EV delivery of SIRT5 mRNA is a promising therapeutic strategy. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.
authors: Wang L, Li W, Sun B, Ouyang Q, Wu X, Luo J, Cui Y, Jiang L, Song M, Cheng J
overview: AIMS: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central pathological drivers of disease progression following traumatic brain injury (TBI).
main: RESULTS: In this study, we demonstrated that TBI promotes neuronal SIRT5 protein degradation via a synergistic regulatory mechanism involving USP7 and TRIM21.

title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity.
abstract: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

title: Engineered Vascularization: Neurovascular Niche Remodeling Enables Biomimetic Brain Organoids for Central Nervous System Research.
abstract: Preclinical central nervous system (CNS) disease models face a persistent translational gap arising from interspecies differences and limited representation of the human neurovascular microenvironment. Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids provide a human-relevant platform for modeling brain development and disease, but limited vascularization restricts tissue growth, maturation, and neurovascular function. Engineering approaches, including genetic engineering, biomaterials, 3D bioprinting, and organ-on-a-chip technologies, enable greater control over vascular specification, spatial organization, extracellular matrix properties, and perfusion, facilitating more controlled remodeling of the neurovascular niche. This Review summarizes recent advances in engineered vascularization of brain organoids, focusing on engineering strategies, biological outcomes, and applications in neurodevelopmental research, CNS disease modeling, and preclinical drug screening. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluating vascularization using complementary evidence rather than individual vascular markers. Based on quantitative data from 13 published studies, we propose the Multidimensional Quality Assessment Framework for Vascularized Brain Organoids (MQAF-VBO) and highlight relationships between engineering parameters and biological outcomes. Emerging opportunities in nanoengineered biomaterials, programmable platforms, spatial profiling, integrated biosensing, and adaptive bioelectronic systems are also discussed. Collectively, these advances may facilitate the development of more reproducible and physiologically relevant vascularized brain organoids for CNS disease modeling and preclinical drug evaluation.

title: Bidirectional Regulatory Mechanisms of T cell-microglia Interactions in Cerebral Ischemic Disease: Molecular Crosstalk, Experimental Techniques and Therapeutic Implications.
abstract: Cerebral ischemic diseases, such as ischemic stroke (IS) and vascular dementia (VaD), are major causes of neurological disability and mortality. Neuroinflammation acts as a pivotal driver of secondary brain injury, mediated by intricate bidirectional interactions between peripheral T cells and central nervous system (CNS)-resident microglia. This review delineates the molecular mechanisms underlying T cell-microglia crosstalk in cerebral ischemia, emphasizing their dual roles in exacerbating neurotoxicity and promoting repair. Direct interactions involve antigen presentation via MHC-TCR engagement and co-stimulatory checkpoints (e.g., CD80/CD86-CD28, PD-L1-PD-1), which regulate T cell activation and microglial polarization. Direct signaling through cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-17, IL-10) further modulates microglial phenotypes: Th1/Th17 cells drive pro-inflammatory M1 polarization via STAT1/NF-κB pathways, while Tregs/Th2 cells induce anti-inflammatory M2 states through STAT6/SMAD signaling. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell omics reveal spatiotemporal dynamics of these interactions, identifying STAT1/STAT6 imbalance as a critical determinant of neuroinflammatory outcomes. Advanced methodologies, including two-photon intravital microscopy and microfluidic blood-brain barrier (BBB) models, enable real-time visualization of immune cell trafficking and synaptic communication. Therapeutically, targeting immune checkpoints (CTLA-4, PD-1) or cytokine pathways (e.g., IL-4 mimetics) shows promise in recalibrating neuroimmune responses. However, challenges such as blood-brain barrier impermeability to biologics and interspecies immune heterogeneity necessitate innovative delivery strategies. This review integrates molecular, cellular, and technological insights to propose a framework for precision immunomodulation. By elucidating context-dependent signaling nodes and leveraging emerging tools, the study underscores the potential of harnessing T cell-microglia crosstalk to mitigate neuroinflammation and enhance neural repair, offering transformative avenues for stroke and dementia therapy.

title: From Intestinal Origins to Mammary Targets: Exploring the Potential Role of the Brain-Gut-Microbiota Axis in Pre-Metastatic Conditioning of Breast Tissue in Colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Historically viewed as a localized gastrointestinal malignancy, colorectal cancer (CRC) is increasingly recognized as a systemic pathology that actively programs distant microenvironments. This review delineates a novel mechanistic framework wherein CRC-driven dysregulation of the brain-gut-microbiota axis (BGMA) acts as a systemic architect of the breast pre-metastatic niche (PMN). We synthesize how localized intestinal oncogenic stress propagates through three convergent conduits: (1) Immune Reprogramming, where gut-derived inflammatory mediators and extracellular vesicles (EVs) recruit myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) to the mammary stroma; (2) Neuro-ecological Conditioning, involving chronic hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activation and sympathetic hyperactivation that drives catecholamine-mediated remodeling of breast tissue; and (3) Humoral-Metabolic Convergence, specifically via the "estrobolome" and secondary bile acids that synchronize systemic hormonal levels with local tissue receptivity. By reframing CRC progression as a systemic pathology that potentially preconditions distant, hormone-sensitive environments, we propose the BGMA as a conceptual framework for prospective "systemic interception", outlining roadmaps to neutralize metastatic cascades at their incipient, reversible stages.

title: Modeling Progressive Brain Volume Losses in Chronic Moderate Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: Extensive, but Attenuating.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Progressive brain atrophy has now been widely observed in the chronic stages of moderate-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI), but there is only coarse information regarding its prevalence and magnitude, and whether rate of atrophy accelerates or attenuates across time. We examined these questions in a Canadian inception cohort from the Toronto Rehab TBI Recovery Study. METHODS: N = 123 patients with post-traumatic amnesia ranging from > 1 h to 10 weeks (70%, > 7 days) were administered up to three MRIs at approximately 5 months, 1 year, and 3 years post-injury. N = 32 healthy controls were scanned up to two times on average 14 months apart. Ventricle-to-brain ratio (VBR) was calculated and manual segmentation of the hippocampi (HPC), corpus callosum (CC), and substructures was employed. For each region, annualized rates of progressive atrophy were modeled from approximately 5 months to 1 year and 1 to 3 years post-TBI; proportions of patients with annualized volume losses of 2.5%-5%, 5%-10%, and > 10% were estimated. RESULTS: Mixed-effects longitudinal models estimated robust progressive atrophy in both time windows in all regions compared to controls, but with significant attenuation across windows. In the earlier window, > 10% annualized loss was estimated in 76.2% of patients for VBR, 53.2% for CC, and 25.0% for HPC bilaterally. In the later window, at least 5%-10% annualized loss was estimated in 63.3% of patients for VBR, 49.4% for CC, and 17.7% for right HPC; for left HPC, 6.3% of patients showed at least 2.5%-5% annualized decline. INTERPRETATION: Clinically concerning prevalence and degree of progressive volume losses were observed in the chronic stages of msTBI, with tapering of losses across time, and regional variations. Research is needed to understand and mitigate clinical impact of these declines.

title: The molecular footprint of valproic acid in human hippocampal organoid.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a multifaceted neurodevelopmental condition characterized by neuroinflammation, and disruption in neuronal development. Valproic acid (VPA) is a known environmental risk factor for ASD. Induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs IMR90-4)-derived human hippocampal organoids (hHOs) at 60 days of development were used to investigate VPA-induced changes in mRNA and microRNA (miRNA) profiles. The molecular effects of VPA on hHOs were deciphered by meaningfully integrating the ability of miRNA to regulate expression of their predicted mRNA targets crucial to altering neuroinflammatory pathways. Molecular footprint can be defined as the VPA-induced changes to the miRNA profile resulting in coordinated post-transcriptional (mRNA) regulation of neuronal and inflammatory pathways associated with ASD. Based on the results, the molecular footprint of VPA in hHOs was generated for the first time. These findings highlight the contribution of miRNA-mediated regulatory mRNA networks to VPA-induced neuroinflammation-associated with ASD in hHOs.

title: Absent Septum Pellucidum Without Polymicrogyria or Seizures in TCP1-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
abstract: T-complex protein 1 (TCP1) encodes the TCP1α subunit, one of eight subunits of the chaperonin containing TCP1 ring complex (TRiC). Heterozygous TCP1 variants cause autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay or intellectual disability, seizures, pyramidal or cerebellar signs, and brain malformations, particularly polymicrogyria. However, the reported clinical spectrum remains limited. We report a 4-year-old girl with global developmental delay, speech and motor delay, behavioral dysregulation, microcephaly, hypotonia with core weakness, and a previously unreported heterozygous likely pathogenic TCP1 variant, c.1392delT (p.A465Qfs*3). This frameshift variant is located in exon 11, truncates the final 16.5% of the protein, is predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay, and is absent from gnomAD. Biological parental testing was unavailable, precluding determination of variant inheritance. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated an absent septum pellucidum with mild bilateral frontal sulcation/gyration asymmetry without polymicrogyria; the optic nerves and pituitary were normal. No seizures were documented through age 4 years. Additional findings included bicuspid aortic valve with mild aortic insufficiency, asthma, severe eczema/atopy, and multiple food allergies. This case suggests that the molecular and neuroimaging spectrum of TCP1-related neurodevelopmental disorder may be broader than previously recognized; however, a causal association between TCP1 and absent septum pellucidum cannot be established from a single case. The relationship of the cardiac and atopic findings to TCP1 remains uncertain. Additional cases and functional studies are needed to clarify genotype-phenotype relationships.

title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time.Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

title: Prenatal Maternal Phosphatidylcholine and Children's Behavior and Cognition through 4 Years of Age: Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Increasing popularity of choline supplements may prompt patients to seek advice on safe, effective doses during prenatal visits. Rationale for prenatal phosphatidylcholine supplements stems from the fetal developmental role of α7-nicotinic cholinergic receptor gene CHRNA7, associated with Schizophrenia, Attention Deficit Disorder, and Autism Spectrum Disorder. Fetal brain developmental problems, including those linked to CHRNA7, convey risk for these mental illnesses. Choline derived from maternal phosphatidylcholine intake activates fetal α7-nicotinic receptors, which facilitate brain neurosynaptic development, observed after birth as robust inhibition of cerebral neurophysiological responses to repeated stimuli. A previous study found that maternal prenatal phosphatidylcholine compared to placebo significantly improved newborns' neurophysiology and thereby decreased the children's attention and social withdrawal problems at 40 months of age. OBJECTIVE: To assess whether maternal prenatal phosphatidylcholine compared to placebo in a larger randomized clinical trial supports fetal brain development to decrease childhood attention and social behavioral problems and increase cognitive performance. STUDY DESIGN: A clinical trial at University of Colorado Hospital Prenatal Clinics and affiliated community hospitals randomized 206 women to 9000 mg phosphatidylcholine (the form of choline occurring naturally in food) or placebo from 16 weeks' gestation through delivery. From 18 months to 4 years of age, 142 children were assessed by parents on the Child Behavior Check List 1.5-5-year version (CBCL1.5-5yr). The 2 primary outcomes were Withdrawn and Attention Problems. A secondary outcome was the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence-IV Full Scale Intelligence Quotient (Full Scale-IQ). Cerebral neurophysiological inhibition, assessed soon after birth, confirmed phosphatidylcholine's fetal developmental effects. RESULTS: Prenatal phosphatidylcholine supplements compared to placebo produced fewer children with multiple or pervasive Withdrawn problems and increased WPPSI-IV Full-Scale IQ (mean difference 7.78, 95% CI 1.88, 13.7; p = .010). Attention problems did not decrease significantly. In exploratory analyses, 11 children had CBCL1.5-5yr Autism Spectrum T-scores in the clinical referral range and language deficits typical of Autism Spectrum Disorder, 10 of 71 from women who had placebo and 1 of 71 who had phosphatidylcholine, Risk Ratio 10.0; 95% CI 1.31, 76.1; p = .026. Twelve children had Full-Scale IQ > 120 (>90 %ile), 10 of 54 from women who had phosphatidylcholine and 2 of 49 who had placebo, Risk Ratio 4.54; 95% CI 1.05, 19.7; p = .044. Positive effects were observed regardless of presence or absence of maternal mental disorders. Phosphatidylcholine produced no significant adverse effects or safety problems for women or children. Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and hypertension were not increased. The children had normal physical parameters at birth and through childhood. Several limitations temper the study's findings: effects on Attention problems did not reach significance, parents rated social behavior, and one-third of women were lost between prenatal enrollment and 4-year assessments. CONCLUSION: Prenatal phosphatidylcholine supplements provide safe, effective support of fetal brain development. Comparison of doses from this and previous trials suggests 6300 mg phosphatidylcholine or 900 mg choline, beginning as early as possible in gestation. Outcomes for the children include fewer social withdrawal problems and increased cognitive test performance.

title: Validating gene-brain-behavior associations in autism: A replication study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism is characterized by heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, neuroimaging and genetic profiles. To elucidate the multi-level heterogeneity, Buch et al. (2023) identified biologically meaningful subgroups in Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). However, ABIDE contains non-biological sources of variability due to retrospectively aligned site protocols. To separate biological from site-related variability and test the robustness of these subgroups, we assessed how well their findings replicate in a deeply phenotyped, prospectively collected autism dataset (EU-AIMS LEAP). METHODS: We included 270 autistic (7.5-30.3 years; 73% male) and 216 non-autistic participants (6.9-31 years; 63.4% male) from LEAP. Regularized canonical correlation analysis (RCCA) was conducted between functional connectivity and three clinical measures (verbal IQ [VIQ], and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 [ADOS-2] social affect [SA] and restricted/repetitive behavior [RRB]). Next, subgroups identified by hierarchical clustering based on canonical variates were characterized by behavior, functional connectivity patterns and gene enrichment analyses. RESULTS: Three of four autistic subgroups showed behavioral profiles consistent with the original study. Three subgroups shared stronger thalamocortical connectivity, while all four displayed distinct connectivity involving default mode network (DMN), salience (SN), visual and somatomotor networks. These subgroup-specific connectivity patterns were further linked to autism-associated and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related gene sets. Across preprocessing pipelines, subgroup assignments were partially preserved. Subgroup2 (globally affected behaviors) and Subgroup4 (less social difficulty, but more restricted behavior) retained more consistent behavioral profiles and connectivity alterations, whereas Subgroup1 and Subgroup3 were more sensitive to the precise preprocessing steps. CONCLUSIONS: These four subgroups showed partly consistent behavioral profiles, connectivity alterations and genetic patterns, extending our understanding of the multi-level heterogeneity of autism.

title: Paternal methylphenidate exposure alters sperm miRNAs and induces intergenerational behavioral and transcriptional changes that are largely reversed by washout.
abstract: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Methylphenidate (MPH), a first-line medication, is often used long-term and not routinely discontinued in individuals planning to have children. Guided by the Paternal Origins of Health and Disease framework, in this study, we investigated intergenerational effects of paternal MPH exposure and reversibility of sperm epigenetic changes. Male BALB/c mice received MPH (15 mg/kg) or vehicle for 28 days and were mated with untreated females immediately after treatment (F0-T1) or after a 40-day washout period (F0-T2). Behavioral tests and brain gene expression analyses were conducted in the offspring (F1), and sperm small noncoding RNA (sncRNA) profiles were examined in F0 males. Male offspring in the F0-T1-MPH group showed increased open-arm entry into the elevated plus maze and reduced expression of Maoa, Maob, and Bdnf in the medial prefrontal cortex. These changes were absent in the offspring derived from the F0-T2-MPH group. Sperm sncRNA sequencing identified 5,684 differentially expressed fragments in F0-T1-MPH mice, including marked alterations in miRNA-derived fragments, such as miR-34c-5p and miR-30e-5p. The target genes of these altered miRNAs were enriched in ADHD-related pathways, including axon guidance and Rap1 signaling. After washout, the number of differentially expressed sncRNA fragments decreased to 665, whereas the number of altered miRNA-derived fragments decreased from 383 to 7. These findings suggest that paternal MPH exposure may influence offspring behavior and brain gene expression through sperm miRNA alterations and that these effects are largely reversible following drug withdrawal.

title: Neurobehavioral Profiles and Clinical Consequences of MYT1L-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Insights From the Brain Gene Registry.
abstract: MYT1L-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (MYT1L-NDD) is a rare autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by intellectual disability, global developmental delay, autism, and obesity. Despite growing recognition, prospective and systematic clinical phenotyping remains limited. Here, we present an exploratory analysis of data from 25 individuals with MYT1L-NDD enrolled in the Brain Gene Registry (BGR), a national platform integrating genetic, neurobehavioral, and clinical data. Neurobehavioral assessments were conducted using the Rapid Neurobehavioral Assessment Protocol (RNAP), including virtual adaptations of the Shipley, Developmental Profile-4, ASEBA Child Behavior Checklist, and Vineland-3. Diagnostic and medication data were extracted from structured electronic health records (EHR). MYT1L-NDD participants were compared to the broader BGR cohort. MYT1L-NDD participants exhibited pronounced impairments in nonverbal cognition and adaptive functioning, particularly in motor tasks, communication, and daily living skills. Behavioral assessments revealed elevated rates of autism symptoms, ADHD symptoms, behavioral conduct problems, oppositional defiance, and anxiety. EHR diagnosis data were available for 10 MYT1L-NDD participants. It showed frequent diagnoses of developmental delays, speech and language disorders, intellectual disability, gastrointestinal problems, and obesity. Medication data on five participants indicated common prescription of alpha-2 adrenergic agonists and laxatives. This study provides the first prospective, multi-source characterization of MYT1L-NDD. Findings expand our understanding of MYT1L-NDD phenotypes in a quantitative and systematic manner and support the value of registry-based approaches for understanding rare neurodevelopmental disorders. Larger, longitudinal, age-stratified studies are needed to further define MYT1L-NDD natural history and inform clinical care.

title: Compartmentalized coenzyme A and ferroptosis vulnerability in PKAN and CoPAN.
abstract: Ferroptotic vulnerability may arise from the failure of a local antioxidant defense even when whole-cell metabolite abundance appears preserved. Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN), two forms of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation caused by defects in coenzyme A (CoA) synthesis, provide a genetically defined setting for examining this possibility. We propose that impairment of the mitochondrial CoA pool can weaken a CoA-dependent redox defense without requiring a measurable whole-cell CoA deficit, while regional iron burden and oxidative demand lower the threshold for ferroptotic death. This model could reconcile apparently preserved bulk CoA with selective neuronal vulnerability. It is testable, remains to be validated directly in patient-derived models, and distinguishes mitochondrial CoA availability from total cellular CoA as the disease-relevant variable.

title: What Does a Donor Need to Know? Content Analysis of Informed Consent Documents Used for Brain Organoid Research.
abstract: Donors of cells used to create induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and brain organoids may not understand what brain organoids are, how they will be used, or the long-term implications of the research. Informed consent documents (ICDs) often contain highly technical language and are written at reading grade levels higher than those attained by the target population. Our goal was to evaluate informed consent documents used for brain organoid research. We compared 20 currently active, IRB-approved consent documents to published templates/guidelines for iPSC research consent. Analyzed ICDs adhered to guidelines in explaining risks and benefits, de-identification, commercial potential, storage, and results sharing. However, descriptions of current and future use were lacking in detail, and the average reading level of ICDs far exceeded that of the general population. Our findings suggest additional transparency in ICDs would assist participants in making an informed choice about participation in iPSC and brain organoid research.

title: Metformin partially modulates cisplatin-induced neuronal senescence but does not prevent rat peripheral sensory hypersensitivity.
abstract: Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) is recognized as a contributor to chemotherapy-associated adverse effects, including neurotoxicity. While senolytics have shown promise in alleviating chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), their clinical translation might be hindered by unfavorable safety profiles, shifting interest toward less toxic senomorphics. We investigated the senomorphic potential of metformin (Met) in counteracting cisplatin (Cis)-induced senescence using both an in vitro model of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons (iPSC-MNs) and an in vivo rat model of CIPN. Exposure of iPSC-MNs to Cis induced hallmark features of senescence, including increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and upregulation of senescence-associated markers, as confirmed by immunofluorescence (increased p16INK4a and decreased Lamin B1) and qPCR (CDKN2A, CDKN1A, CXCL8 upregulation) analyses. While Met did not significantly reduce SA-β-gal activity or restore cell viability, it attenuated the expression of key senescence-associated transcripts, including CDKN2A and components of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) such as CXCL8, indicating partial senomorphic activity. In vivo, Cis administered in two cycles (cumulative dose: 23 mg/kg) elicited mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia in Sprague-Dawley rats. Analysis of dorsal root ganglia (DRG) on day 8 post-treatment revealed strong SA-β-gal staining and increased expression of cdkn1a, cdkn2a, and SASP mediators (Il6). Met pretreatment reversed the upregulation of cdkn1a, cdkn2a, and Il6, but did not alleviate the sensory deficits induced by Cis. Our findings support a partial senomorphic activity of Met both in vitro and in vivo yet demonstrate its limited efficacy in functionally mitigating CIPN.

title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes.
abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

title: Exploratory chromosome 14-focused transcriptomic profiling of PSEN1-associated familial Alzheimer's disease across brain regions.
abstract: Familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) is an inherited form of early-onset Alzheimer's disease associated with pathogenic variants in presenilin 1 (PSEN1). To explore chromosome 14-associated transcriptional patterns in FAD across anatomically distinct brain regions, publicly available RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) datasets from frontal cortex, temporal cortex, and whole-brain samples were analyzed. Because one FAD sample and one control sample were available for each brain region, expression differences were evaluated descriptively using observed log₂ fold-change values rather than conventional inferential differential-expression statistics. Functional annotation and protein-protein interaction analyses were subsequently used to provide biological context for the observed expression patterns. Distinct regional expression patterns were observed within the chromosome 14-focused dataset. Higher expression was observed for representative genes including FITM1, IFI27, AHSA1, and NFKBIA in the frontal cortex, and DHRS4L2, ESR2, GPR65, EFCAB11, and HOMEZ in the temporal cortex. The observed expression patterns were associated with inflammatory, cellular stress, metabolic, receptor-mediated, proteostatic, and neuronal signaling-related functions. Network analysis was used to contextualize these expression patterns rather than to infer causal regulatory relationships. Five representative proteins-NFKBIA, ESR2, GPR65, AHSA1, and IFI27-were further examined structural information to provide structural context for selected transcriptomic observations. Given the absence of biological replication and the chromosome 14-focused design, these findings should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Independent replicated cohorts and complementary transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional studies are required to determine the reproducibility and biological relevance of the observed patterns.

title: Loss of CRMP4 in astrocytes causes reduced scar formation and functional recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Reactive astrocytes play a central role in shaping the post-injury microenvironment after spinal cord injury (SCI), yet the molecular mechanisms governing their proliferative expansion and contribution to scar architecture remain incompletely defined. Conditional deletion of CRMP4 in astrocytes significantly reduced astrocyte proliferation, altered scar organization, and attenuated the inflammatory milieu surrounding the lesion, including reduced microglial activation. These changes were accompanied by significantly improved locomotor recovery, as assessed by the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) locomotor rating scale, indicating enhanced functional restoration after SCI. Our findings suggest that CRMP4 promotes the expansion of reactive astrocyte subsets that shape the inhibitory niche surrounding the lesion core, thereby restricting axonal regeneration and limiting functional recovery after SCI. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of a public dataset revealed that Crmp4 expression is enriched in proliferative, progenitor-like astrocyte subpopulations that contribute to scar formation, including subclusters corresponding to the G2/M phases of the cell cycle. Together, this study identifies astrocytic CRMP4 as a key molecular determinant of reactive astrocyte dynamics and scar architecture after SCI, providing new insight into cell-type-specific regulation of glial responses in central nervous system injury.

title: Essential Oils From the Fruit of Amomum villosum Lour. Alleviate LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation by Repressing PI3K-Akt and MAPK Signaling Pathways.
abstract: Amomum villosum Lour. has been traditionally valued in various cultures for its health benefits. Here, we show that the neuroprotective effects of the essential oils extracted from the fruit of Amomum villosum Lour. (AVEO) and elucidate its underlying mechanisms in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammation. The main compounds of AVEO can cross the blood-brain barrier and significantly improve cognitive and behavioral dysfunction in LPS-induced mice, leading to a 50% enhancement in Morris water maze performance, a 60% and 80% reduction in immobility time in the tail suspension test and forced swimming test, respectively. Moreover, AVEO mitigates neuron loss and suppresses the expression of pro-inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, while upregulating the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 in brain tissue. RNA-seq and metabonomics analyses reveal that AVEO modulates multiple inflammation-related pathways and restore metabolic homeostasis in brain tissue. Remarkably, AVEO attenuates hyperactivation of the PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling pathways in LPS-induced microglia and improves neuronal damage in LPS-induced microglia-neuron co-culture system. Altogether, our findings suggest that AVEO alleviates neural dysfunction by modulating PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling cascades and promoting metabolic reprogramming upon neuroinflammation, thereby revealing the therapeutic potential of AVEO in several neurological disorders.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid positive for SARS-CoV-2 associated with neurological manifestations and proteome alterations in a multiple myeloma patient.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although SARS-CoV-2 infection is primarily associated with respiratory symptoms, neurological complications have been increasingly recognized, even in the absence of pulmonary involvement. CASE PRESENTATION: We report a case of a 67-year-old woman with a history of multiple myeloma and recent exposure to a COVID-19-positive individual who developed rapidly progressive neurological symptoms, including dysarthria, dysphagia, and hypoesthesia, without any respiratory manifestations. Her condition deteriorated to focal and dyscognitive status epilepticus, requiring mechanical ventilation. Brain MRI showed imaging features consistent with rhombencephalitis. SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed through positive qRT-PCR results from both nasopharyngeal swab and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Further analysis of the CSF using quantitative shotgun proteomics via mass spectrometry revealed a neuroinflammatory profile indicative of blood-brain barrier disruption and differential expression of several proteins relevant to brain function, including the major prion protein, superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD-1), and other aggregation-prone proteins. CONCLUSIONS: This case supports the hypothesis that SARS-CoV-2 can invade the central nervous system and cause severe neurological impairment, even in the absence of typical respiratory symptoms. The findings underscore the importance of considering SARS-CoV-2 in the differential diagnosis of rapidly progressive neurological syndromes and highlight the need for further investigation into the mechanisms of neuroinvasion and the potential neurotropism of emerging viral variants.

title: Youth Mental Health-Related Emergency Department Visits After Hurricane Helene: A Difference-in-Differences Analysis.
abstract: PURPOSE: Extreme weather can disrupt social supports, schooling, and access to behavioral health services, potentially affecting youth mental health. This study examined changes in youth mental health-related emergency department (ED) visits following Hurricane Helene (2024). METHODS: ED surveillance data from North Carolina (2022-2024) were used to assess mental health-related visits among youth aged 5-26. A difference-in-difference (DID) design compared FEMA-designated disaster counties with nondeclared counties before and after the storm. Multilevel intersectional analyses evaluated risk by sex, race/ethnicity, age, and insurance. RESULTS: Anxiety-related ED visits increased in disaster-exposed counties post-Helene (DIDRR = 1.14, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.01-1.29), with larger increases among females than males (DIDRR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.03-1.35). Depression also showed greater relative increases among females (difference-in-difference-in-differencesRR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.09-1.51). Self-harm visits declined overall (DIDRR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.52-0.94). DISCUSSION: Hurricane Helene was associated with shifts in youth mental health-related ED use, demonstrating the need to strengthen adolescent and young adult behavioral health services in disaster-prone rural communities.

title: Imaging-Enhanced Prediction of Upper Limb Motor Function After Stroke Using Automated Segmentation and Cluster Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, and early prediction of motor outcomes is critical for guiding individualized rehabilitation strategies. Although neuroimaging offers prognostic insights, its clinical integration remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether explainable imaging-derived features can improve the prediction of upper limb motor impairment and to identify distinct recovery profiles through cluster analysis. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 242 patients with acute ischemic stroke who underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and motor function assessment. Clinical and imaging variables-including infarct volume, motor tract involvement, and subtype classification-were extracted using automated software. Predictive models for Fugl-Meyer Assessment upper extremity (FMA-UE) scores were developed using hierarchical regression, and K-means clustering was applied to standardized baseline data. Cluster characteristics were compared, and recovery profiles were visualized. RESULTS: Incorporating imaging variables improved prediction of FMA-UE scores (adjusted R²: 0.595), with motor tract lesion volume emerging as a key predictor. Cluster analysis revealed three distinct patient subgroups: Cluster 1 (mild impairments, younger age), Cluster 2 (older patients with multiple comorbidities), and Cluster 3 (severe neurological deficits, large infarcts). Functional outcomes differed significantly across clusters, with Cluster 3 showing the greatest disability (76% with follow-up modified Rankin Scale 4-6, P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Imaging-derived features from early magnetic resonance imaging improve the prediction of upper limb motor outcomes after stroke. Cluster-based stratification identifies clinically meaningful subgroups, supporting precision rehabilitation through personalized care planning and targeted secondary prevention.

title: A practical one-electrode electrochemical methodology for tracking catalyst reconstruction in NiFe-Prussian blue analogues for the oxygen evolution reaction.
abstract: Efficient and durable alkaline oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts are essential for large-scale water electrolysis, yet the dynamic reconstruction of precatalysts into their true active phases remains difficult to track with simple, broadly accessible tools. Here, we use NiFe Prussian blue analogues (NiFe-PBA) grown on nickel foam (NF) as a model system to develop a practical, fully sequential one-electrode workflow that correlates structural evolution with electrochemical kinetics during the OER. NiFe-PBA/NF electrodes with varying Ni : Fe stoichiometries are synthesized hydrothermally and optimized for OER performance, identifying NiFe-PBA 1 : 1/NF as the best-performing composition. A continuous one-electrode protocol is then applied to the same physical electrode, enabling us to monitor reconstruction and kinetic stabilization under realistic operating conditions. Post-OER analysis reveals substantial disruption of the NiFe-PBA framework, amorphization, and increased Ni3+/Fe3+ and oxyhydroxide species, consistent with the formation of a NiFeOOH-like active phase. By directly linking these structural and surface-chemical changes to the observed kinetic improvements, this study clarifies the role of NiFe-PBA as an electrochemically transformable precursor to NiFeOOH and demonstrates a simple, accessible one-electrode approach for tracking catalyst reconstruction and active-phase evolution in alkaline OER.

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

title: Automated Multi-class Segmentation of Mandibular Odontogenic Cysts and the Mandibular Canal on CBCT Images Using a Hybrid Deep Learning Framework.
abstract: Mandibular odontogenic cysts can complicate surgical planning if located near the mandibular canal. Accurate delineation of both structures is therefore clinically important. This study presents a deep learning-based method for simultaneously segmenting mandibular odontogenic cysts and the mandibular canal in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images. The developed method relies on a hybrid deep learning architecture integrating a ConvNeXt-Base encoder, a Dilated Context Block, a U-Net-based decoder, and a Deep Supervision mechanism. This framework simultaneously segments the mandibular canal and odontogenic cyst regions within the same architecture, promoting multi-scale contextual feature learning. We evaluated the performance of the proposed method using fivefold cross-validation experiments on a real-world clinical CBCT dataset comprising 103 patient images. We assessed segmentation performance using overlap-based metrics together with boundary-aware HD95 and ASSD metrics. The experimental results demonstrated that the model achieved a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 76.28% ± 1.83%. Excluding the background class yielded macro IoU and macro F1-score values of 64.46% ± 2.74% and 77.00% ± 1.89%, respectively. Meanwhile, the weighted IoU and weighted F1-score values were 78.71% ± 4.25% and 87.63% ± 2.63%, respectively. In boundary-based evaluations, the mandibular canal had an HD95 of 2.44 ± 2.98 mm and an ASSD of 0.45 ± 0.30 mm. The corresponding values for odontogenic cysts were 5.59 ± 3.65 mm and 1.43 ± 0.88 mm, respectively. These results suggest that the mandibular canal is more consistently delineated, while cyst segmentation remains more challenging, particularly at irregular and low-contrast boundaries. The proposed framework allows for the simultaneous and objective segmentation of mandibular odontogenic cysts and the mandibular canal within a unified, multi-class CBCT analysis framework. By providing reproducible delineation of both structures, this method could serve as a technical foundation for future quantitative analyses of lesion-canal relationships. However, further validation using larger, multicenter, volumetric CBCT datasets is required before clinical translation.

title: Annotation-Efficient Individual Muscle Segmentation from Dixon MRI: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark of Pretraining and Fat-Fraction Guidance.
abstract: Measuring individual muscles and their fatty infiltration on Dixon MRI can support sarcopenia assessment, but manual annotation is time-consuming and annotated datasets are often small. This study investigated accurate individual-muscle segmentation with limited labelled data. Three datasets were used: an abdominal CT dataset of 300 subjects with adipose-tissue labels, a lower-limb Dixon MRI dataset of 25 subjects with 13 thigh and 9 calf muscles, and an independent cohort of 66 subjects for external testing. Network architecture, encoder pretraining, a Dixon-derived fat-fraction input, and a shared CT-MRI encoder were compared. A 2.5D model, subject-level cross-validation, zero-shot transfer, label-free domain adaptation, and few-shot adaptation were also evaluated. The best models reached Dice 0.947 ± 0.017  for CT adipose tissue and 0.925 ± 0.010  for thigh muscle; the best 2.5D model reached 0.928, while a reported 3D Attention-Res-V-Net reached 0.857 under a different protocol. Encoder pretraining helped most at the smallest budgets, with ImageNet performing best and comparably to CT-based pretraining at eight subjects. A shared CT-MRI encoder retained accuracy with 44 %  fewer parameters, and thigh-muscle volumes agreed closely with reference measurements (ICC ( 2 , 1 ) = 0.998  ). On the external cohort, fine-tuning raised Dice from 0.11 zero-shot to 0.61, 0.76, and 0.88 with four, eight, and 46 labelled target subjects. The fat-fraction input improved segmentation only when very few subjects (two or four) were labelled. Encoder pretraining and efficient model sharing help when annotated MRI data are scarce. A small amount of target-domain annotation substantially improves cross-cohort transfer, and repeated subject-level validation is important for reliable evaluation.

title: Wavelet Scalogram-Based Nystagmus Classification for Automated Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo Subtype Diagnosis.
abstract: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vestibular vertigo, yet accurate diagnosis remains challenging without specialist expertise. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-based diagnostic algorithm for BPPV using video-nystagmography (VNG) recordings. A total of 1352 VNG recordings were collected from patients with posterior semicircular canal (PSCC) BPPV (n = 234), lateral semicircular canal (LSCC) BPPV (canalolithiasis, n = 188; cupulolithiasis, n = 58), and healthy controls (n = 224) at a single tertiary referral hospital, yielding 1738 signal segments (1312 nystagmus segments annotated by two otolaryngologists and 426 normal segments). Eye trajectory signals were extracted using a deep learning-based VNG eye-tracking algorithm, transformed into two-dimensional (2D) scalogram representations via continuous wavelet transform (CWT), and classified using task-specific backbone architectures selected through systematic comparison under a patient-level data split. Ablation analysis showed that CWT-based 2D representations significantly outperformed raw one-dimensional (1D) time-series baselines. The final models achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values of 0.974 for horizontal and 0.961 for torsional nystagmus classification. For BPPV subtype diagnosis, recording-level accuracy was 0.935 for the PSCC and 0.938 for the LSCC evaluation; F1-scores exceeded 0.84 for all PSCC classes and ranged from 0.59 to 0.98 for LSCC classes, with canalolithiasis variants outperforming cupulolithiasis variants. These findings suggest the feasibility of AI-assisted BPPV diagnosis from VNG recordings.

title: Combined eye tracking and electroencephalography during referential selection in dyadic interaction.
abstract: Understanding language in real-world interaction requires methods that integrate auditory, visual, and neural signals. We present a proof-of-concept study combining mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking to investigate referential selection during dyadic communication. Using a simplified version of the director task, pairs of participants engaged in naturalistic object-movement instructions while EEG and gaze data were recorded and synchronized via LabStreamingLayer, allowing us to calculate overlap-corrected, regression-based event-related potentials (rERPs) time-locked to spoken nouns and to participants' fixations, focusing on the N400/P300 (300-500 ms) and later (500-800 ms) time windows. Our results show that gaze behavior and fixation-related potentials provide crucial information for interpreting language-related ERPs: Targets competing with occluded referents elicited a stronger posterior positivity consistent with greater attentional demands. Fixation timing systematically modulated neural responses. Contrary to predictions, competitors received little visual attention, indicating that participants prioritized task-relevant information. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal data integration for understanding attentional and predictive mechanisms in real-world communication. Importantly, we show that established analytic techniques, such as artifact subspace reconstruction, independent component analysis, and linear deconvolution for ERP calculation, apply to noisy, naturalistic datasets. In addition, we provide a subsampling sensitivity approach to test the stability of the effects across different sample sizes. This study provides a methodological framework linking gaze and neural activity during interactive language processing. All preprocessing and analysis scripts, along with example datasets, are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/5ds4z ; a modified and optimized Python implementation is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/XlinCLab/DGAME ).

title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells.
abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca2+ dynamics. Removing Ca2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain.Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

title: Exercise promotes lipophagy and mitigates cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease through downregulating microglial TMEM9.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction contributes to lipid droplet (LD) accumulation, which drives pathological progression in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Exercise is reported to restore autophagy-lysosomal function and attenuate cognitive impairment in AD, but its regulation of LD deposition remains unknown. METHODS: 5×FAD transgenic mice underwent a three-month exercise intervention. Cognitive and emotional behaviors were assessed using the Morris water maze, novel object recognition, and open field test. LD deposition was evaluated by oil red O and BODIPY staining. Proteomic sequencing was performed to identify proteins affected by exercise. Pathological changes were examined by immunofluorescence, western blotting, and transmission electron microscopy. Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV was used to overexpress or knock down microglial TMEM9 to investigate the mechanisms by which physical exercise affects behavior and pathology in AD. In vitro, BV2 cells were cultured and incubated with oligomeric amyloid-β (oAβ), with or without oleic acid to induce LD formation. Chloroquine and rapamycin, which regulate autophagy-lysosomal function, were used to examine the effects of LDs on mitochondrial integrity under glucose deprivation conditions. Lentiviral or plasmid transfection was used to explore the key role of TMEM9 in regulating lipophagy, and the interaction between TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 was detected by co-immunoprecipitation. Clinically, plasma TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 levels in AD patients were measured by ELISA, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate diagnostic performance. RESULTS: Exercise mitigated cerebral LD deposition through enhanced lipophagy, preserving mitochondrial integrity and attenuating cognitive decline. Mechanistically, exercise suppressed microglial TMEM9 expression, restoring LD degradation. Tmem9 downregulation facilitated LKB1 lysosomal translocation, activating AMPK signaling. In vitro, oleic acid-induced LDs preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and increased ATP production in BV2 microglia under glucose deprivation and oAβ exposure. Tmem9 overexpression exacerbated lipophagy impairment and mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas Tmem9 knockdown enhanced lipophagy and cytoprotection. Aβ clearance was negatively regulated by TMEM9. Clinically, AD patients exhibited characteristic Aβ deposition and glucose hypometabolism, with plasma TMEM9 levels strongly correlating with p-tau217 progression. Plasma TMEM9 and the TMEM9/ATP6AP1 ratio emerged as potential AD diagnostic biomarkers (AUC=0.791 and 0.853, respectively). CONCLUSION: These findings establish exercise-induced TMEM9 inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy targeting lipidostasis to combat AD progression.

title: Shared cortical morphometry and molecular signatures across depression and physical diseases.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly comorbid with physical diseases, suggesting shared neurobiological mechanisms. However, the common structural and molecular substrates underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. We analyzed multimodal MRI data from 577 patients (MDD, asthma, fibromyalgia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, type 2 diabetes) and 275 healthy controls, constructed individual morphometric similarity networks (MSN) to identify shared cortical alterations, and applied principal component analysis with multiscale molecular annotation (transcriptomic, cell-type, neurotransmitter, and cognitive mapping) to characterize underlying mechanisms. All patient groups exhibited regional MSN abnormalities. A shared MSN pattern emerged, featuring increased similarity in visual and somatomotor regions and decreased similarity in ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and was replicated in independent cohorts. This pattern was significantly associated with spatial gene expression enriched for synaptic signaling, membrane potential regulation, and neuronal architecture, with predominant expression in excitatory/inhibitory neurons and astrocytes. It further mapped onto specific neurotransmitter systems, with exploratory cognitive decoding suggesting possible relevance to emotion and social cognition. Related genes overlapped with known risk loci for Alzheimer's disease and bipolar disorder. These findings identify a robust across diseases cortical MSN phenotype linked to convergent molecular and neurochemical correlates, offering a framework for studying shared vulnerability and transdiagnostic mechanisms across depression and physical diseases.

title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.
authors: Peng S, Wang L, Ouyang J, Liu R
overview: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells.
main: Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: The translational asymmetry of corpus callosotomy: Two literatures that answered different questions.
abstract: Corpus callosotomy is an established palliative operation for drug-resistant epilepsy dominated by drop attacks, and it is performed in three extents: anterior, usually of the anterior two-thirds; total, in one or two stages; and selective posterior, which preserves the genu and rostral body. Meta-analysis finds no difference between them in overall seizure reduction, a difference in drop attack control favoring the posterior approach, and a graded difference in disconnection syndrome, but there has never been a prospective head-to-head comparison, and the optimal extent of section remains undefined. A search of PubMed, Embase, and the Web of Science Core Collection identified 62 experimental studies in which the corpus callosum or another forebrain commissure was sectioned with an epilepsy-related outcome, spanning 1948-2026 across six species and every major seizure model. This literature is neither absent nor recent. What it has almost never done is vary the extent of section: the few studies that varied it took the laterality of kindling transfer or of interictal synchrony as the endpoint, never seizure control and never cognitive cost. No study compares the three extents against a common outcome; none models the selective posterior operation as it is defined clinically; none randomizes between extents; and none combines graded disconnection with time-locked bilateral electrophysiology, diffusion-based verification of the fibers divided, and a behavioral read-out in the same animals. The effect of section is also bidirectional: focal seizures may intensify through loss of transcallosal inhibition, and in the pentylenetetrazol model callosal section paradoxically facilitates convulsions, which limits chemoconvulsant preparations. The asymmetry between the clinical and experimental literatures is therefore one of method rather than of volume or attention: the two answered different questions, and the question the clinical field now asks requires a manipulation the experimental literature has never performed. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Surgeons can treat severe epilepsies by cutting the bundle of fibers that joins the two halves of the brain, but they do not agree on how much of it to cut. We searched three databases and found 62 animal studies of this operation going back to 1948. Almost none of them compared different amounts of cutting, and none looked at the newest version of the operation. Answering the surgeons' question will require a new kind of animal experiment rather than more reading of the old ones.
