title: Pushing the limits of atomic force microscopy: Emerging methods for speed, resolution, and quantitative analysis.
abstract: Since its introduction 40 years ago, atomic force microscopy (AFM) has transformed nanoscale imaging across the physical and life sciences. In biology, AFM has provided unprecedented insights into nanoscale biomolecular organisation under near-physiological conditions, revealing structures and interactions inaccessible to many conventional approaches. However, biological function is inherently dynamic, and understanding molecular mechanisms requires moving beyond static structural snapshots towards direct observation of processes across multiple spatial and temporal scales. In this review, we discuss emerging approaches that are extending the capabilities of AFM beyond traditional imaging, pushing the limits of temporal resolution, spatial precision, quantitative measurement, and data analysis. We highlight advances in speed that enable direct visualisation of molecular dynamics, approaches for sub-millisecond measurements, methods that overcome conventional resolution limits, and computational approaches that enhance image analysis, automation, and information extraction from complex datasets. Together, these developments are transforming AFM from a technique focused primarily on high-resolution structural imaging into a platform for dynamic, quantitative, and high-throughput investigation of biological systems. Finally, we consider how these advances may shape the next 40 years of AFM, enable autonomous measurements and reveal biological mechanisms across previously inaccessible spatial and temporal scales.

title: Secondary electron imaging in transmission electron microscopy: technique and application in nanocatalysis.
abstract: The determination of the smallest structures and surface morphologies of nanoparticles using Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) is widely regarded as one of the most essential techniques for modern researchers. Despite its proven scientific effectiveness, TEM has certain limitations, the main one of which is that the analysis of nanoparticles or their agglomerates - in fact three-dimensional structures - results in two-dimensional images, which may not fully reflect their complex geometries. A promising solution to this problem lies in the integrated on modern TEM devices secondary electron (SE) detectors. These detectors, optimized for capturing low-energy secondary electrons, function similarly to those in Scanning Electron Microscopy. Complementing high-resolution TEM or STEM images, the SE detector provides three-dimensional images with a resolution close to or equal to atomic, while allowing avoidance of the labor-intensive and time-consuming processes associated with TEM-based 3D tomography, for example. With current advancements in detector technology, secondary electron imaging holds significant potential as a primary tool for investigating the morphology of a wide spectrum of nanomaterials, including nanoparticles and powders, paving the way for broader applications in nanoscience and materials research. In this review, we will briefly cover the features of the method and its main physical principles, and recent advances in its application in nanocatalysis with platinum group metals-based catalysts, where the application of this method could be revolutionary. The distribution of metal nanoparticles on the carbon or other support is a critical factor directly affecting the performance of these materials. And, as practice shows, traditional TEM often fails to provide comprehensive information on their morphology.

title: MD2-IN-1 restores microglial lysosomal function and attenuates amyloid pathology through TREM2-associated signaling in 5×FAD mice.
abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a central regulator of microglial adaptation during Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the development of small-molecule modulators associated with TREM2 signaling remains limited. Here, through a consensus pharmacophore-guided virtual screening strategy, MD2-IN-1 was identified as a candidate small molecule associated with TREM2 signaling. Biolayer interferometry and cellular thermal shift assays supported cellular target engagement related to TREM2 (KD = 13.85 μM). In Aβ-stimulated BV2 microglia, MD2-IN-1 increased SYK phosphorylation, promoted Aβ uptake, and shifted microglial responses toward a less proinflammatory phenotype. These effects were markedly attenuated following Trem2 knockdown, indicating the involvement of the TREM2-SYK signaling pathway. Mechanistically, MD2-IN-1 restored lysosomal acidification and increased the expression of the V-ATPase subunits ATP6v0c and ATP6v0a1, accompanied by increased intracellular Aβ degradation. In 5×FAD mice, chronic MD2-IN-1 administration improved cognitive performance without detectable behavioral abnormalities compared with WT animals. Multimodal PET imaging demonstrated reduced amyloid deposition and attenuated neuroinflammatory signals, which were further supported by histological analyses showing decreased plaque burden, reduced inflammatory microglial responses, and preserved neuronal integrity. In addition, MD2-IN-1 reduced P62 accumulation and restored ATP6v0c expression in vivo, whereas these effects were partially attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of TREM2. Collectively, these findings identify MD2-IN-1 as a small-molecule modulator associated with TREM2 signaling that restores microglial lysosomal degradative function and promotes Aβ clearance in AD models, providing pharmacological support for targeting adaptive microglial responses in AD.

title: The neuropathy-causing GARS1∆ETAQ mutation drives pathology in subsets of motor and sensory neurons in mice.
abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D (CMT2D) results from gain-of-function mutations in GARS1, which encodes glycyl-tRNA synthetase (GlyRS), the enzyme responsible for charging transfer RNA (tRNA) with glycine. There are several CMT2D mouse models, but Gars∆ETAQ/+ is the only one that bears a patient-sourced mutation. Created using CRISPR/Cas9 to model a 12-nucleotide de novo GARS1 deletion identified in an unusually severe CMT2D patient, Gars∆ETAQ/+ mice have previously been shown to display several neuromuscular phenotypes: motor axon loss, denervated neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) and reduced muscle function. Here, we extend these analyses to provide a more comprehensive understanding of both motor and sensory nerve deficits across hind- and fore-limbs. At 3 months, Gars∆ETAQ/+ mice possess sex-independent alterations in the levels of neuropathy biomarkers - including decreased NfL and increased periaxin - alongside reduced muscle endurance and strength, and impairments in the sensory modalities of mechanosensation, proprioception and nociception. Underpinning these dysfunctions, we identified site-specific defects comprising altered sensory neuron populations, muscle spindle loss, reduced motor neuron size, disrupted NMJ innervation and maturation, and reduced axonal transport of signalling endosomes in vivo. Together, these experiments show that Gars∆ETAQ/+ mice display robust and selective peripheral nerve pathology that manifests in a general length-dependent fashion, priming this CMT2D allele for testing treatments and evaluating mechanisms underlying peripheral nerve vulnerability.

title: Beyond PROTACs: Conditional Technologies and New Frontiers.
abstract: This chapter surveys the post-PROTAC landscape of targeted protein degradation (TPD), covering conditional activation, new degradation modalities, and proximity-driven editing of post-translational modifications (PTMs). Condition-activated PROTACs harness prodrugs responsive to irradiation or the tumor microenvironment and nanoparticle-based platforms to achieve spatiotemporally resolved protein degradation. The targetable space is further expanded by molecular glues that recruit neosubstrates to E3 ligases, endocytosis-lysosome targeting chimeras that clear extracellular and membrane proteins, and autophagy-lysosome strategies that degrade aggregates and damaged organelles. Ribonuclease-recruiting chimeras achieve targeted RNA degradation, while the induced-proximity concept is repurposed for PTM regulation, enabling targeted glycosylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation and dephosphorylation via the recruitment of glycosyltransferases, acetyltransferases, and kinases and phosphatases. Future advances in all-small-molecule-based conditional systems, brain-targeted delivery, and regulatory frameworks informed by degradation kinetics will embed stimulus sensing and logic-gated operations into intelligent molecular systems, shifting the paradigm toward on-demand proteome and transcriptome rewiring for precision medicine.

main: Future advances in all-small-molecule-based conditional systems, brain-targeted delivery, and regulatory frameworks informed by degradation kinetics will embed stimulus sensing and logic-gated operations into intelligent molecular systems, shifting the paradigm toward on-demand proteome and transcriptome rewiring for precision medicine.

title: Levetiracetam restores GABAergic function and network homeostasis following Vps35 deficiency in excitatory neurons.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) remain incurable, partly due to their complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms. Loss of vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein 35 (VPS35), a core component of the retromer complex, has been implicated in AD and ADRDs. While Vps35 deficiency is known to increase amyloidogenesis by regulating its cargo proteins, such as APP and BACE1, the precise mechanism by which VPS35 dysfunction leads to cognitive impairment remains elusive. While neuronal VPS35 regulates trafficking and functions of multiple synaptic membrane proteins, such as postsynaptic glutamatergic and GABAnergic receptors and pre-synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, and Levetiracetam (LEV), an antiepileptic drug that improves cognition, interacts with the SV2A, exactly how LEV enhances cognition is still a matter of debate. METHODS: Given the abundant expression of VPS35 in pyramidal excitatory neurons, we generated a conditional knockout mouse model with Vps35 deletion from postnatal glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Vps35CaMKIIα) and characterized its phenotypes using a combination of behavioral assessments, and electrophysiological, biochemical, and immunohiotological analyses in the hippocampal CA1 region. A targeted pharmacological screen was conducted to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LEV. RESULTS: Vps35 deletion did not disrupt the gross brain development but led to progressive cognitive decline beginning at three months of age. Electrophysiological analyses revealed earlier-onset hippocampal CA1 hyperexcitability, marked by depolarized resting membrane potentials and reduced Kir2.1 expression. However, restoring Kir2.1 to suppress hyperexcitability failed to rescue cognitive deficits. Instead, cognitive impairment was associated with weakened GABAergic transmission and disruption of the excitatory/inhibitory balance in the Schaffer collateral-CA1 circuit. Notably, LEV treatment diminished these deficits in mutant mice. Intriguingly, LEV increased the levels of retromer component, VPS26A, and multiple pre- and postsynaptic GABAergic proteins, in addition to SV2A, all of which were reduced in Vps35-deficient CA1 neurons. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify VPS35 in excitatory neurons as a critical factor for inhibitory synapse maintenance and network homeostasis. This study also highlights LEV as a potential therapeutic strategy for ADRDs through the preservation of GABAergic synapses.

title: Distribution of doublecortin in the developing retina of birds: A comparative analysis.
abstract: The avian retina presents an elegant and highly accessible model for investigating the spatial and temporal dynamics of neurogenesis within the central nervous system. In recent years, the microtubule cytoskeleton has emerged not merely as a structural scaffold, but as a dynamic regulator of the transition of a morphologically homogeneous pool of multipotent progenitor cells to postmitotic neurons. Doublecortin (DCX) is a microtubule-associated protein broadly recognized for its fundamental roles in neuronal migration, differentiation, and structural plasticity within the developing nervous system. While its roles in the brain are well-documented, the precise spatiotemporal distribution of DCX in the developing retina of birds remains poorly understood. In this study we investigated the expression pattern of DCX during embryonic development of the retina of one altricial (zebra finch, Taeniopygia guttata) and two precocial (chicken, Gallus gallus; Japanese quail, Coturnix coturnix) bird species using immunohistochemical techniques. Our results demonstrated that the onset of DCX expression coincided chronotopographically with the onset of neurogenesis in the developing retina. In these early stages, DCX expression is tightly colocalized with the neuronal marker class III β-tubulin. As retinal histogenesis progressed to more advanced stages, DCX expression persisted and segregated into specific subsets of ganglion, amacrine, and horizontal cells. Furthermore, prominent immunoreactivity was maintained within the ciliary marginal zone (CMZ), highlighting its association with late-stage retinal progenitors and ongoing neurogenesis. These findings reveal a conserved spatiotemporal expression pattern of DCX across diverse avian species. Furthermore, it suggests that some elements of the cytoskeleton and its associated regulatory proteins form a functional continuous biological continuum: first acting as drivers of neurogenesis and migration and, subsequently, transitioning into structural stabilizers that lock in and maintain the complex morphology of fully differentiated, mature retinal neurons.

title: Chrysanthemum Morifolium-Derived Nanovesicles Reduce Lactate-Associated Histone Lactylation and Modulate Microglia-Mediated Neuroinflammation in Sepsis-Associated Encephalopathy.
abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE)-a complication of the central nervous system in patients with sepsis-markedly diminishes cognitive functions and is linked to hippocampal neuritis-induced injury. Plant exosome-like nanovesicles can transport proteins, lipids, and molecular compounds between neural cells and the periphery, thereby modulating target cells. This study examined the therapeutic potential of Chrysanthemum morifolium-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (CRELNVs) in an animal model of lipopolysaccharide-induced SAE, revealing their ability to effectively cross the blood-brain barrier, be internalized by microglia, and alleviate nerve injury and memory impairment by reducing lactate levels in microglia at the hippocampus. CRELNVs decreased lactylation levels in microglia, thus promoting the conversion of microglial cells from the detrimental M1 metabolic phenotype to the protective M2 one. Mechanistically, our finding suggest CRELNVs reduced proinflammatory cytokine release is associated with the inhibition of NF-κB activation. Thus, CRELNVs were concluded to exert their protective effects by modulating the H3K18la/NF-κB axis and regulate microglia-mediated neuroinflammation by responding to the hippocampal neuritis-induced injury in SAE.

title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

title: The Evolving Paradigm of Autism: Folate Receptor Autoimmunity deranging Epigenetic Programming in fetal and postnatal Brain Development.
abstract: This review on autism provides a summary of the multiple genetic, epigenetic and environmental changes setting the stage for disturbed brain development due to aberrant synaptogenesis and corticogenesis during the prenatal and post-natal periods. The emphasis is placed on nonmendelian transmission driven by epigenetics. Folate deficiency appears to play a critical role in influencing many of the structural changes contributing to developmental deficits. Impaired passage of folate across the placental and the blood-brain barriers to the fetal and postnatal brain because of folate receptor autoantibodies (FRAb) emerges as the major cause. Cerebral folate deficiency with or without autism has been associated with FOLR1 gene defects, a rare disorder. On the other hand, FRAb in association with low CSF folate is present in most children diagnosed with autism. These autoantibodies are present in more than 1/3 of asymptomatic parents of children with autism or are acquired by the child during the first two years of life. Early detection of FRAb amongst autistic children is necessary to enable high dose folinic acid treatment. The use of folinic acid before conception and during pregnancy among mothers or both parents with FRAb, represents a promising strategy to reduce the risk of autism in future offspring. Interventational treatments in parents prior to pregnancy and optimal therapeutic approaches in infants are needed to prevent disordered development of the pre- or post-natal brain.

title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

title: The ferroptosis-neuroinflammation feedback loop in traumatic brain injury: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability worldwide, with secondary injury processes such as ferroptosis and neuroinflammation adding to its detrimental effects. Recent studies reveal a profound bidirectional interaction. On one hand, inflammation drives ferroptosis by disrupting iron homeostasis through the IL-6/Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)-hepcidin axis, impairing the system Xc-/glutathione (GSH)/GPX4 antioxidant system and promoting immune cell infiltration. Conversely, ferroptotic cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) and lipid peroxidation end-products like 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), which activate toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and fuel a neuroinflammatory vicious cycle. We further discuss emerging therapeutic approaches targeting this axis, including ferroptosis inhibitors (Fer-1, Lip-1), dual-regulatory agents (annexin A5, melatonin, and H2S), and exosome-based delivery systems, while highlighting translational difficulties presented by the BBB and complex time windows. This review presents a framework to comprehend the interplay between ferroptosis and inflammation and to guide the development of dual-targeted treatments in TBI.

title: PTPRS mediates invasion of tetanus neurotoxin into the central nervous system.
abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT) invades the central nervous system (CNS) via retrograde transport through motoneurons. Whether a host factor is needed to mediate TeNT trafficking has remained unknown. Here, using pull-down and mass spectrometry analysis, and by developing a luciferase-based in vivo transport assay, we identify receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPRS; PTPσ) as the retrograde transport receptor for TeNT. Global or motoneuron-specific PTPRS knockout (KO) abolishes TeNT entry into the CNS in mouse models. PTPRS-TeNT interactions occur in endosomes, prevent toxin translocation, and direct TeNT trafficking in neurons. Structural studies establish that the TeNT light chain and belt region bind to the immunoglobulin domain of PTPRS. Disrupting TeNT-PTPRS interactions blocks TeNT trafficking into the spinal cord; consistently, a PTPRS-binding-deficient TeNT mutant induces botulism-like flaccid paralysis. Thus, PTPRS is the host factor mediating TeNT trafficking into the CNS, revealing a targetable pathway for post-entry intervention and drug delivery into the CNS.

title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

title: Nanotechnology meets neurodegeneration: restoring lysosomal function with nanovectors.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) remain a growing burden worldwide. Characterized primarily by degeneration of neurons in the central nervous system (CNS), driven in part by pathological protein aggregates and by alterations of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP), current therapeutic strategies only mitigate the outcomes of NDs rather than their origin, highlighting the need for the development of new targeted therapies. AREAS COVERED: CNS-targeted nanoparticles (NPs) to tackle ALP have offered promising avenues by bypassing biological barriers, reducing pathological protein aggregates, restoring lysosomal pH and activity, upregulating autophagic flux, and contributing to neuroprotection. This report summarizes recent advances in the development of CNS‑targeted nanocarriers for autophagy as a treatment for ND. EXPERT OPINION: Restoring ALP function is a promising disease-modifying strategy for NDs, as it helps clear toxic protein aggregates. Nanotechnology offers an effective way to deliver such therapies to the brain by overcoming the blood-brain barrier, enabling targeted, multimodal, and potentially cell-specific interventions. However, key challenges remain, including late diagnosis, the need for precise cell targeting, and concerns about long-term safety and bioaccumulation. Despite these limitations, growing research interest is expected to accelerate the development and clinical translation of these approaches.

abstract: In this issue, Aiken et al. Their findings suggest that balanced KIF1A activity is required for proper synaptic development and function.

title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

title: Conformational allocation of mitofusin 2 in neuronal mitochondrial dynamics: Mechanisms and therapeutic targeting.
abstract: Neurons must sustain functional mitochondria far from the cell body. Mitofusin 2 (MFN2), a dynamin-like large guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase), coordinates outer mitochondrial membrane remodeling with axonal transport, bioenergetic support, inter-organelle communication, and stress-responsive quality control. Studying these activities separately obscures how disruption of one protein produces diverse neuronal phenotypes. We propose a testable conformational-allocation framework in which molecular state distributions and transition kinetics bias MFN2 participation across cellular outputs. Integrating structural and functional evidence, we distinguish experimentally resolved mechanisms from working models. Variants associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) are compared by the molecular step or functional output affected. Fusion loss alone does not capture this mechanistic diversity. Structure-guided docking supports local compatibility at a shallow, conformationally conditional C-terminal surface, without establishing native accessibility, affinity, or therapeutic response. CMT2A provides the strongest context for intervention, combining causal genetics, direct mitofusin engagement studies, and multiscale rescue. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) provides secondary preclinical evidence, whereas Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases remain exploratory. The mitofusin pathway is chemically tractable, but paralog selectivity and state-dependent target engagement remain unresolved. A state- and variant-informed strategy may better match intervention to the affected output than indiscriminate enhancement of fusion.

title: A scoping review of infant body composition (0-24 months) assessed by deuterium dilution.
abstract: CONTEXT: The deuterium dilution technique is applicable across the 0-24 month age range in diverse resource settings. No structured review has previously mapped the scope of its use in this population. OBJECTIVE: This scoping review was limited to mapping infant body composition studies (0-24 months) using deuterium dilution, describing methodological approaches, identifying contexts of applications, and highlighting evidence gaps. METHODS: A structured literature search was conducted across four databases with citation tracking, following prisma-ScR guidelines. RESULTS: Twenty-four studies from approximately 18-20 distinct cohorts across six continents were included from 1,078 identified records. Substantial heterogeneity was documented in every protocol element: dose, equilibration time, analytical platform, correction factor for non-aqueous exchange (unreported in approximately one-third of studies), and hydration model. This heterogeneity prevents direct comparison of fat mass and fat-free mass values across studies, precluding meta-analytic synthesis. Key gaps include the near-absence of data in preterm infants (one study), small for gestational age (SGA) or intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) classification in only three of 24 studies, and incomplete breastfeeding documentation. CONCLUSION: This review maps a growing but methodologically heterogeneous literature. Standardised protocol reporting, dedicated preterm and SGA studies, and longitudinal designs linking early body composition to later outcomes are research priorities.

title: The ferroptosis-lipid metabolism-neuroinflammation axis in Alzheimer's disease: A review of mechanistic interplay and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves multiple pathological pathways, with ferroptosis and lipid metabolic dysregulation forming a coupled mechanism across the disease course, and neuroinflammation acting as a key mediator. While existing reviews often focus on isolated processes, they frequently lack an integrative analysis of the "ferroptosis-lipid-neuroinflammation axis" as a systemic pathological core. This review specifically addresses this gap by proposing a unified mechanistic framework for neuronal injury, synaptic dysfunction, and immunometabolic remodeling in AD, centered on this tripartite axis. We comprehensively summarize how key pathways involving glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), the cystine/glutamate antiporter system Xc-, solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), and N6-methyladenosine (m6A) regulation shape neuroinflammation within this context. Furthermore, we explore how advanced methodologies, including spatial omics, single-cell transcriptomics, organoid models, and engineered exosome methods, are instrumental in elucidating regional specificity, optimal intervention windows, and targeted delivery strategies for modulating this iron-lipid-inflammation interplay. This axis functions as a pathological amplifier, linking metabolic, oxidative, immune, and structural dysfunctions. Its systemic reprogramming offers a new paradigm for AD subtyping, biomarker discovery, and multitarget interventions, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional amyloid-β/tau-centric approaches. This review integrates literature published up to the submission date, ensuring the inclusion of the latest mechanistic insights and translational advances in the ferroptosis-lipid metabolism-neuroinflammation axis.

title: HSV-1 induces stable associations between the Golgi and endosomes within the cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment of neuronal cells.
abstract: Assembly of mature herpesvirus particles is associated with extensive rearrangement of cytoplasmic membranes. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection in neuronal cells induces the formation of a distinctive cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment (cVAC), in which rearranged host membranes and viral proteins are clustered at the perinuclear microtubule-organizing center (MTOC). Although both the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and endosomal compartments have been implicated as membrane sources for cytoplasmic envelopment, how secretory and endosomal pathways are reorganized and associated within the cVAC remains unclear. Here, we treated HSV-1-infected cells with nocodazole at a post-entry stage to disperse membrane components of the cVAC and identify microtubule-independent membrane organizations and associations using immunofluorescence imaging. We found that the Golgi apparatus was fragmented during infection but maintained cisternal stacking, as the Golgi markers GM130, GalT, and GRASP65 remained colocalized in both the absence and presence of nocodazole. We further demonstrated that Golgi mini-stacks retained their association with Rab6 during HSV-1 infection and formed microtubule-independent associations with early and recycling endosomes, resulting in the formation of Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks. Viral capsid, glycoprotein, and tegument proteins were colocalized with Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks in both the presence and absence of microtubules, suggesting that this membrane complex serves as a site of cytoplasmic envelopment regardless of clustering at the MTOC. Formation of these stable Golgi-endosome associations did not require viral capsids. Neither actin filaments nor acetylated microtubules colocalized with Golgi-endosome super-mini-stacks, suggesting that cytoskeletal elements are not required for this association.IMPORTANCEMany viruses remodel host cytoplasmic membranes to facilitate their assembly. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying this remodeling may reveal novel antiviral targets while also providing insight into fundamental principles of intracellular membrane organization. Infection with an important human pathogen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), induces extensive membrane remodeling that leads to the formation of the cytoplasmic viral assembly compartment (cVAC) in neuronal cells, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that HSV-1 induces stable associations between membranes within the cVAC. Our findings support a model in which HSV-1 generates a dynamic hybrid membrane compartment during infection, potentially reconciling conflicting views on the roles of distinct membrane sources in cytoplasmic assembly.

title: Transcriptomic analysis reveals distinct expression patterns in focal cortical dysplasia.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a common cause of drug-resistant epilepsy in children and adults and exhibits substantial clinical and histopathological heterogeneity. However, morphological classification alone does not fully explain variability in epileptogenicity, disease severity, or treatment response. METHODS: We aimed to define molecular mechanisms underlying FCD heterogeneity using integrated transcriptomic and regulatory analyses. RNA and small RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) were conducted on cortical tissue resected during epilepsy surgery from 66 patients with histopathologically confirmed FCD subtypes IA (n = 17), IIA (n = 25), and IIB (n = 24), along with 15 postmortem cortical control samples. Differential expression and weighted gene coexpression network analysis were used to identify coordinated transcriptional programs, and microRNA (miRNA) profiling was integrated to assess posttranscriptional regulatory mechanisms. Integrative multivariate analyses (DIABLO and sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis) were used to evaluate subtype discrimination, and findings were validated using an independent RNA-seq dataset. RESULTS: FCD subtypes showed distinct but partially overlapping molecular profiles. FCD IA showed a comparatively subtle transcriptional profile, dominated by reduced expression of genes involved in cortical development, neuronal signaling, ion regulation, and metabolic stress. FCD IIA displayed a modest yet coherent molecular signature involving developmental and neuronal disruption, together with metabolic stress and autophagy. FCD IIB exhibited the most extensive transcriptional remodeling, including activation of antigen presentation pathways, complement activation, cytoskeleton reorganization, synaptic alterations, and extracellular matrix organization. Differential miRNA profiling identified shared miRNAs, including miR-320 family, miR-27a-5p, miR-142-5p, and miR-21-5p, alongside subtype-specific regulatory patterns. Integration of messenger RNA and miRNA data revealed concordant alterations, indicating that miRNA dysregulation may contribute to stabilization of subtype-specific transcriptional states. SIGNIFICANCE: These findings demonstrate that FCD is characterized by coordinated transcriptional and posttranscriptional network alterations that extend beyond morphological classification and may contribute to variability in epileptogenicity across subtypes.

title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. title: Functionalized Silica-Coated Metallic Replicas of Intracellular Protein Assemblies.
abstract: To replicate hierarchical biological architectures, biotemplating leverages diverse biological structures as templates for inorganic materials. Among the various inorganic materials explored in biotemplating, silica is an attractive material because of its stability and biocompatibility. However, existing biotemplating methods are largely nonselective, yielding silica replicas of bulk biological specimens. Here, we report an approach for selective materialization of targeted protein-associated architectures from cells and tissue slices, enabling recovery of the resulting silicified structures after enzymatic removal of surrounding non-target biomolecular components. To this end, we (i) immunolabeled target proteins with fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, (ii) embedded specimens in a hydrogel, (iii) removed endogenous proteins via enzymatic digestion, and (iv) converted the retained fluorophore patterns into Au nanoparticle assemblies through fluorophore-directed nanogold labeling and electroless Au growth, followed by silica coating. Using this strategy, we fabricated microtubule-derived silica bioreplicas from a human immune-lineage cell line and tuned their overall size by adjusting the expansion of the surrounding hydrogel matrix. Furthermore, functionalization of the silica surface with magnetic nanoparticles enables controlled motion of the bioreplicas under electromagnetic actuation. Finally, we extended the method to mouse brain slices and produced thermally stable silica bioreplicas of astrocytic and oligodendrocytic structures. Overall, this work expands the structural diversity and selectivity of silica-based biomimetic materials and broadens the palette of biotemplating templates.

title: Human-Derived Motor Neuron Progenitor Cell Implantation Rescues Motor Endplates Following Peripheral Nerve Injury.
abstract: PURPOSE: Degradation of motor endplates (MEPs) following peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is a major determinant of functional recovery, as prolonged denervation renders target muscles progressively unreceptive to reinnervation. While prior studies have demonstrated that stem cell-based therapies may provide neurotrophic support following PNI, their potential effects on MEP preservation have not been well studied. We hypothesized that transplantation of human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived motor neuron progenitors (MNPs) into chronically denervated muscle would be associated with preservation of MEP architecture. METHODS: With Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee approval, chronic denervation injuries were created in mice via sciatic nerve transection. After 4 months of denervation, when MEPs have consistently degraded in this animal model, the denervated tibialis anterior (TA) was injected with low-dose MNPs (10,000 cells), high-dose MNPs (500,000 cells), or phosphate-buffered saline (negative control). Using a previously established method, hiPSCs were differentiated into functional MNPs prior to injection. At selected time points post-injection, the TA was harvested and immunostained to confirm MNP viability and detect the presence of MEPs. RESULTS: Transplanted MNPs remained viable within host muscle at both evaluated time points. No identifiable MEPs were detected in phosphate-buffered saline-treated chronically denervated muscle. In contrast, MNP-treated muscles demonstrated the presence of MEP-like structures following prolonged denervation. Qualitative differences in MEP density and morphologic complexity were observed between treatment groups, with greater preservation seen in the higher-dose cohort. Contralateral uninjured muscles demonstrated intact native MEP architecture. CONCLUSIONS: Intramuscular transplantation of hiPSC-derived MNPs into chronically denervated muscle was associated with preservation of MEP morphology in this preclinical proof-of-concept model. These preliminary findings suggest that cellular therapies may represent a potential adjunctive strategy to preserve end-organ receptivity following delayed peripheral nerve injury. TYPE OF STUDY/LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Preclinical controlled animal study, Level V.

title: Double periodicity of the AnkyrinG-associated complex in the axon initial segment.
abstract: The axon initial segment (AIS), situated within the first 20 to 60 µm of the axon, is essential for action potential generation and maintenance of axonal identity [M. N. Rasband, Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 11, 552-562 (2010)]. Its structure relies on the beta (β)-IV-spectrin/AnkyrinG (AnkG) scaffold arranged periodically underneath the plasma membrane, harboring diverse membrane proteins [K. Xu, G. Zhong, X. Zhuang, Science 339, 452-456 (2013); K. L. Hedstrom, Y. Ogawa, M. N. Rasband, J. Cell Biol. 183, 635-640 (2008)]. Although a ~190-nm cytoskeletal periodic organization is well established, the precise stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of AIS proteins within the ~190-nm spatial period remain rudimentary, mostly for lack of sufficient spatial resolution and labeling efficiency. Here, using expansion microscopy and cryoelectron tomography, which overcome these technical limitations, we present data on the organization of the AnkG-associated complex within the ~190-nm spatial period. We demonstrate that exactly two AnkG molecules are situated within each period and with their C termini separated by ~80 nm. By contrast, the AnkG-associated cell-adhesion protein neurofascin-186 appears in clusters of varying sizes that are consistent with the periodic organization of AnkG pairs, yet suggesting a more complex molecular arrangement between the two molecules. Altogether, our approach provides insights into AIS molecular organization and protein stoichiometry.

title: Inhibition of glycan sialylation reduces amyloid-β secretion via suppression of amyloid-β exocytosis.
abstract: Among nutrient-sensitive regulatory mechanisms, protein glycosylation is a key post-translational modification that links metabolism to protein function. Amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Because excessive accumulation of Aβ is believed to drive AD progression, approaches that reduce Aβ production and secretion remain of considerable therapeutic interest. Accumulating evidence suggests that protein glycosylation influences the processing and trafficking of amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) and other proteins involved in Aβ metabolism. However, while N-linked protein glycosylation has been shown to affect Aβ production, the specific contribution of protein terminal glycan sialylation remains incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of inhibiting glycan sialylation on Aβ production using CHO cells stably expressing human APP. Treatment with the sialyltransferase inhibitor P-3Fax-Neu5Ac (P-3Fax) significantly reduced extracellular Aβ levels, while intracellular Aβ levels were increased. Importantly, P-3Fax treatment did not alter β-secretase- or γ-secretase-mediated cleavage of their substrates, indicating that changes in secretase activity do not account for the reduction in extracellular Aβ. In addition, P-3Fax treatment markedly reduced plasma membrane levels of lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1), consistent with impaired lysosomal exocytosis. Taken together, these results indicate that inhibition of sialylation by P-3Fax reduces extracellular Aβ levels independently of secretase activity, potentially through impaired lysosomal exocytotic pathways. Our findings identify glycan sialylation as a key regulatory factor in Aβ trafficking and provide new insight into the cellular mechanisms controlling Aβ homeostasis.

title: Renal stress-associated extracellular vesicle signaling linked to lysosomal cathepsin D and NEK7-NLRP3 neuroinflammation.
abstract: Systemic exposure to neurotoxins such as 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) affects both the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral organs; however, the contribution of peripheral organ stress to neuroinflammation remains incompletely understood. Here, we propose a peripheral-to-central signaling mechanism in which renal stress-associated extracellular vesicles (EVs) are linked to microglial inflammasome activation. Using computational and biochemical approaches, cathepsin D (CTSD) was identified as a molecular target of the MPTP metabolite 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP +). MPP + accumulated in renal tissue and was associated with lysosomal stress and tubular injury, accompanied by increased release of circulating EVs enriched with renal injury markers. Pharmacological inhibition of pepstatin A-sensitive lysosomal protease activity attenuated renal injury and EV release. MPTP exposure was also associated with blood-brain barrier disruption, potentially permitting circulating EV-associated signaling to influence the CNS. Plasma-derived EVs isolated under MPTP-treated conditions were associated with increased microglial activation, whereas pharmacological inhibition of EV biogenesis attenuated this response. Mechanistically, EV exposure was associated with inflammatory responses involving NIMA-related kinase 7 (NEK7)-NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3-associated inflammatory signaling and IL-1β maturation. Consistent with these findings, NEK7 deficiency attenuated microglial activation and dopaminergic neuron loss in vivo. Together, these findings suggest that renal stress-associated EVs may be involved in linking peripheral stress to central neuroinflammatory responses. This study provides a tentative but verifiable framework for renal stress-EV-inflammasome communication in toxin-induced neuroinflammation.

title: Autophagy-Modulating Nanomedicine for Glioma: Delivery Barriers, Lysosomal Interactions, and a Flux-Resolved Translational Decision Framework.
abstract: Glioma nanomedicine is constrained by linked delivery and pharmacodynamic barriers: nanoscale systems must traverse heterogeneous blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) interfaces and achieve interpretable intracellular effects in tumor cells. Autophagy is a therapeutically relevant but context-dependent axis. However, similar changes in static autophagy markers, vesicular staining, or ultrastructure can reflect productive autophagy induction (ie, increased autophagic flux with successful lysosomal cargo degradation), blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal dysfunction, or secondary cytotoxic stress. This ambiguity is amplified for nanomedicines because their physicochemical properties can independently shape autophagy-related readouts. Here, we frame autophagy-modulating nanomedicine for glioma as both a delivery challenge and a problem of translational interpretation, covering bioactive nanomaterials, nanocarriers, and multimodal platforms. We organize the field around an integrated framework linking BBB/BBTB access, intracellular trafficking, interpretation of autophagic flux, and translational readiness. We use structured evidence grading to distinguish flux-resolved, functionally validated mechanisms from marker-based or indirect inferences. This framework distinguishes mechanistically supported findings from provisional interpretations and defines the evidence required for translational progression.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle-Mediated Antifungal and Immunomodulatory Therapy for Neuromycoses.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neuromycoses, fungal infections affecting the central nervous system (CNS), cause approximately 112,000 deaths annually, representing 19% of AIDS-related deaths globally. Conventional antifungal drugs are limited by poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, systemic toxicity, and increasing drug resistance. Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as promising vehicles for enhancing antifungal efficacy while modulating immune responses. Thus, this comprehensive review synthesizes current knowledge on LNPs as vehicles for antifungal immune modulators, including their design principles, drug delivery mechanisms, physiological interactions, translational potential, and roadmap for next-generation precision medicine approaches to treating neuromycoses. METHODS: A comprehensive narrative review of original studies on LNP-based approaches for neuromycoses was conducted. The literature was synthesized using a structured evidence table encompassing six studies published between 2019 and 2026, including one randomized clinical trial in adults, one case report, one in vitro study, two animal studies, and one study incorporating both in vitro and in vivo approaches. Original research studies were prioritized, while reviews, commentaries, and editorials were excluded. FINDINGS: This review shows four principal findings: (1) LNP formulations achieved mean fungicidal activity of 0.402 log1 0 CFU/mL/day, non-inferior to intravenous amphotericin B, with 18-week survival and reduced toxicity compared to intravenous formulations; (2) LNPs cross the BBB with limited or no systemic toxicity while enabling intracellular trafficking through optimization of lipid composition and surface chemistry; (3) RMT demonstrates high specificity affected by variability in receptor expression, while AMT and TMT operate through distinct mechanisms with their own potential off-target effects; and (4) encapsulation reduces nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity compared to free antifungal drugs, with amphotericin B-loaded NLC showing reduced nephrotoxicity in vitro compared to conventional formulations. CONCLUSION: These findings highlight the potential of LNP-based antifungal delivery and the need for further clinical validation before broader clinical translation.

title: Exercise, DNA methylation, and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic links and future directions in intergenerational research.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia and remains without a cure; recently introduced disease-modifying therapies provide only modest slowing in selected patients. Physical exercise is associated with better cognitive and functional outcomes, but the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain incompletely understood. DNA methylation is a potential interface linking environmental stimuli to gene regulation and neural function. This narrative review examines evidence connecting exercise, DNA methylation, and AD, with emphasis on AD-related loci and on the possible intergenerational implications of parental exercise. We examine methylation findings involving amyloid precursor protein (APP) and presenilin-1 (PSEN1), which are relevant to amyloid-β production; microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT), which encodes tau; and apolipoprotein E (APOE), which influences lipid transport and amyloid-β clearance. These findings suggest potential epigenetic contributions to AD-related biology, although their direction and functional significance vary across studies. We also discuss exercise-responsive pathways involved in energy sensing, autophagy, and redox signaling. We also evaluate whether exercise-associated epigenetic remodeling could influence amyloid-β accumulation, Tau homeostasis, and neuronal function. Evidence that exercise modifies DNA methylation is growing, whereas studies that integrate exercise interventions, genome-wide methylation, and AD-related outcomes remain scarce. Evidence for an inherited reduction in AD susceptibility is even more limited and currently supports a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism. Future studies integrating behavioral, neuropathological, cell-type-resolved epigenomic, and other multi-omic outcomes are needed to determine whether exercise-induced DNA methylation changes mediate neuroprotection in AD or primarily reflect broader physiological adaptation.

title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

title: Hydrogel-mediated local PTK2 inhibition promotes ordered axonal regeneration associated with cytoskeletal remodeling after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Disorganized axonal regrowth after spinal cord injury (SCI) may compromise the spatial organization and directional alignment of regenerating axons. Our previous COL6-modified hydrogel model revealed physical guidance-independent, self-organized spinal cord regeneration, whose neuron-intrinsic mechanisms remain unclear. Using proteomic screening of a COL6-modified hydrogel model that promotes ordered spinal cord regeneration, we identified protein tyrosine kinase 2 (PTK2) as a candidate intracellular regulator associated with axonal organization. In vitro, PTK2 downregulation by siRNA or pharmacological inhibition with PF-573228 reduced neurite tortuosity and branching and increased radial directional coherence. Exploratory long-read transcriptomic analysis, together with Western blotting, revealed coordinated changes in integrin-, RhoA-, cofilin-, and actin-related signaling after PTK2 inhibition, consistent with cytoskeleton-associated remodeling. To achieve localized PTK2 inhibition in vivo, PF-573228 was incorporated into an injectable thiol-modified hyaluronan/gelatin hydrogel, termed HaG-PF, which exhibited porous microarchitecture and hyaluronidase responsiveness. In a mouse model of complete spinal cord transection, HaG-PF was associated with reduced p-PTK2 at the 4-week endpoint, increased NF200+ axonal presence, improved two- and three-dimensional axonal organization, increased CGRP+ fibers within the lesion site, and the presence of 5-HT+ fibers in the caudal stump. Improved axonal organization was accompanied by enhanced locomotor and electrophysiological recovery. Collectively, these findings identify local PTK2 inhibition as a molecular strategy for promoting more organized axonal regeneration after SCI.

title: Reprogramming pathological secretory phenotype of chondrocytes inhibits neurovascular invasion for osteoarthritis treatment.
abstract: Pain severity in osteoarthritis (OA) often dissociates from the extent of cartilage structural damage, indicating that non-structural mechanisms contribute to symptom persistence. Here, we identify articular chondrocytes as active orchestrators of pathological neurovascular invasion through a pathogenic secretome, rather than merely passive victims of degeneration. Integrated human single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals that OA chondrocytes undergo phenotypic reprogramming characterized by coordinated activation of angiogenic and neurotrophic programs. Functionally, inflammatory chondrocytes directly promote endothelial angiogenesis and sensory axon outgrowth, linking chondrocyte-derived signals to neurovascular invasion and sustained pain. To therapeutically target this upstream mechanism, we engineered MMP-13-responsive celecoxib-loaded hyaluronic acid methacrylate microspheres (HMPC) for disease-adaptive delivery to degenerative cartilage. HMPC suppresses chondrocyte COX-2 activity and remodels the pathological chondrocyte secretome through restoration of miR-339-5p_R-5 and miR-103-3p_R-2, thereby inhibiting angiopoietin-2 (Angpt2)-mediated angiogenesis and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf)-driven sensory neurogenesis. In murine OA models, HMPC markedly alleviates pain-related behaviors, reduces neurovascular infiltration, and preserves joint structure. Collectively, this study supports a chondrocyte-centric framework in which reprogrammed chondrocytes govern neurovascular invasion through microRNA-dependent secretome regulation and introduces a smart biomaterial-enabled strategy with disease-modifying potential for OA pain intervention.

title: Olive leaf-derived exosome-like vesicles attenuate neurotoxicity in an in vitro rotenone model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease primarily characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation. Despite extensive research, current therapeutic options remain limited to symptomatic management, underscoring the need for neuroprotective strategies targeting disease pathology. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective potential of exosome-like vesicles derived from olive (Olea europaea) leaves (Ole-ELVs) in an in vitro PD model induced by rotenone in SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells. To evaluate the protective impact of olive leaf-derived ELVs, oxidative stress, cell viability, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation were assessed by measuring reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential staining, and Thioflavin S staining for α-synuclein aggregation. Our findings indicate that treatment with Ole-ELVs significantly attenuated rotenone-induced ROS production, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced protein aggregation. Collectively, these results suggest that Ole-ELVs exert neuroprotective effects through antioxidative, protection against cytotoxicity, and mitochondrial-stabilizing mechanisms, offering a promising natural nanoscale therapeutic candidate for PD.

title: [A case of bilateral open-lip schizencephaly with West syndrome due to variant of PAFAH1B1 gene and literature review].
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To report the clinical manifestations, genetic features, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of a child with bilateral open-lip schizencephaly complicated by West syndrome due to a variant of PAFAH1B1 gene, and review the relevant literature. METHODS: Clinical data of a 4-month-old boy were retrospectively analyzed, and 35 previously reported cases were systematically reviewed. This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Gansu Provincial People's Hospital (Ethics No.: 2025-871). RESULTS: The 4-month-old boy presented with clustered flexor spasms, hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalography, and developmental regression. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed bilateral pachygyria, schizencephaly, and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. Trio whole-exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous NM_000430.4: c.703_704delAG (p.Glu235Metfs*20) frameshift variant in the PAFAH1B1 gene. Sanger sequencing confirmed that neither parent carried this variant. Based on the guidelines from American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), the variant has met the criteria for PVS1+PS2_Moderate+PM2_Supporting, and was classified as pathogenic. After treatment with adrenocorticotropic hormone combined with vigabatrin and other antiseizure medications, the epileptic spasms were controlled and the electroencephalographic abnormalities had improved. However, global developmental delay persisted at the 12-month follow-up. Analysis of the present case and 35 previously reported cases showed that PAFAH1B1-related phenotypes were highly consistent, mainly including infantile spasms (28/36), developmental delay/intellectual disability (29/36), and abnormal brain MRI findings (30/36), predominantly cortical malformations. The reported variant types included deletions, frameshift variants, nonsense variants, missense variants, and splice-site variants. CONCLUSION: PAFAH1B1 gene variants are an important cause for cortical malformations, including schizencephaly, and may lead to secondary West syndrome. This study has systematically summarized the genotypic and phenotypic features of bilateral open-lip schizencephaly complicated by West syndrome associated with a frameshift variant of the PAFAH1B1 gene. For infants with epileptic spasms or early-onset epilepsy accompanied by structural brain abnormalities, early genetic evaluation should be performed, and antiseizure treatment should be integrated with neurodevelopmental rehabilitation to facilitate long-term management.

title: Multiple motor proteins regulate TDP-43 anterograde axonal transport.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is an RNA-binding protein essential for RNA metabolism. Under physiological conditions, it predominantly resides in the nucleus but is also expressed in the cytoplasm, where it regulates mRNA trafficking and local translation. In nearly 97% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases, TDP-43 undergoes nuclear depletion and cytoplasmic aggregation. While its nuclear functions are well characterized, its axonal roles remain poorly understood, despite axonal degeneration being a hallmark of ALS pathology. To address this gap, we investigated TDP-43 localization and transport dynamics in axons of H9-derived human neurons. We compared fluorescently labeled TDP-43 with three well-characterized axonal cargoes, ras-related protein Rab5, synaptophysin, and amyloid precursor protein, and examined protein-protein interactions between TDP-43 and the axonal transport machinery. Our analyses revealed that TDP-43 exhibits active anterograde axonal transport and interacts with multiple kinesin motor proteins, including all three KIF5 isoforms, through the adaptor KLC1, and the synaptic vesicles motor KIF1A. This multi-motor engagement suggests a flexible transport system that ensures mRNA delivery to distal axons. In ALS, where TDP-43 accumulates abnormally in the cytoplasm, this flexibility may become compromised, with multiple transport mechanisms simultaneously affected. This could contribute to progressive accumulation of non-functional TDP-43 granules, disrupting mRNA trafficking and local translation. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding how physiological TDP-43 transport mechanisms may be impaired during disease, highlighting axonal TDP-43 transport pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: The IKC-leptin axis functions as a molecular bridge between neurodevelopment and endocrine signaling.
abstract: Kcnb1-null mice exhibit hypoleptinemia, disrupted Kcnb1-integrin-K+ channel complex (IKC) interactions with the leptin receptor (LepR) in proopiomelanocortin neurons, and broad neurodevelopmental and cognitive abnormalities. Because leptin is neurotrophic and IKC-LepR assemblies are present in neocortex, we tested whether leptin modifies these phenotypes. Early-life leptin supplementation partially improved behavioral and cognitive deficits and more strongly corrected anatomical and neuronal abnormalities. In null cortical neurons, leptin normalized dendritic overgrowth and F-actin dynamics through LepR- and integrin-dependent mechanisms. WT animals and neurons showed modest leptin responses; however, integrin manipulation unmasked leptin sensitivity, whereas LepR blockade induced null-like defects without exogenous leptin. These findings support a dual-mode model in which LepR signaling is regulated by both ligand availability and IKC-dependent mechanisms, identifying IKC-LepR coupling as a molecular interface linking endocrine signaling to neocortical development.

title: Non-muscle actinopathy-associated loss-of-function actin variants modulate cytoskeletal reorganization.
abstract: Variants in ACTB gene encoding for cytoplasmic β-actin result in a group of rare disorders called non-muscle actinopathies (NMA). A subgroup of NMA patients with ACTB pLoF (predicted loss-of-function) disorder have various congenital malformations, such as microcephaly and intellectual disability. We investigated the cellular effects of an ACTB pLoF missense variant, G302A, and a four-amino-acid deletion, S338-I341 in cytoskeletal β-actin, in patient-derived fibroblast cells. We found that neither of the mutations affected the organization of actin or the width of the actin-filament bundles, while the mutation G302A reduced the stiffness of the cells as measured by using atomic force microscopy. The latter effect might be associated with the misorganization of tubulin and with the increased size and number of focal adhesions. When we challenged the cells by monolayer stretching and followed the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, we found that G302A mutant cells showed denser actin filament bundles within the cells compared to wild type cells. At the same time, the extent of cofilin reorganization from the cell periphery was increased upon stretch, and this correlated with an increased cofilin phosphorylation. In the case of deletion, while the extent of cofilin phosphorylation increased, the extent of reorganization was unaltered; rather, the phosphorylation of myosin light chain, important in counteracting external force, was reduced by 75%. We could partially rescue this effect by overexpressing the active form of the formin mDia1. Our findings open the possibility to verify the cellular phenotype in the most affected patients' cells, in neurons.

title: From iPSC disease modeling to epigenome editing: Toward therapeutic reversal of genomic imprinting disorders.
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and organoids are increasingly important components of new approach methodologies because they provide experimentally accessible human systems that preserve patient-specific genetic backgrounds and can be differentiated into disease-relevant cell types. Genomic imprinting disorders are particularly attractive targets for this approach because their pathogenesis depends not only on DNA sequence but also on parent-of-origin-specific epigenetic regulation. Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) and Angelman syndrome (AS), which arise from distinct disruptions within the same imprinted domain on chromosome 15q11.2-q13, illustrate both the opportunities and the complexity of therapeutic epigenetic manipulation. Recent studies using PWS patient-derived iPSCs have shown that disease-associated imprinting states are largely retained after reprogramming and can be experimentally reversed by locus-specific epigenome editing. Targeted demethylation of the PWS imprinting control region restored multiple paternally expressed genes, and the corrected state persisted after differentiation into hypothalamic organoids, partially normalizing disease-associated transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Here, we discuss how iPSC-based disease modeling is evolving from a platform for mechanism discovery toward a test bed for therapeutic epigenome engineering and outline the major challenges that must be addressed before epigenome editing can be translated to patients with imprinting disorders.

title: Model Systems infrastructure of the German Center for Mental Health (DZPG): toward an integrated, mechanism-based framework for mental health research.
abstract: Mental health is fragile and disorders are highly prevalent arising from complex interactions between genetic, developmental, psychological, social and environmental factors. The key mechanisms underlying resilience, vulnerability factors, brain repair systems, and recovery remain poorly understood, hindering the development of effective prevention and personalized treatment. The German Center for Mental Health (Deutsches Zentrum für Psychische Gesundheit, DZPG) addresses these challenges through a nationwide, interdisciplinary research network that integrates basic science with translational approaches across multiple sites. Its embedded "Model Systems" infrastructure provides a state-of-the-art platform to investigate brain-behavior mechanisms. Animal models are available to explore the links between genes, neural circuits, and behavior. Additionally, humanized model systems are established based on transgenesis and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based models. Brain organoids further support research into neurodevelopment and multicellular interactions.Critically, when combined with high-content/high-throughput screening, iPSC-derived models link disease mechanisms to therapeutic targets. Advanced techniques, such as machine learning-based behavior quantification, single-cell and spatial multi-omics analyses, and genome editing enable in-depth analysis of disease/patient-specific cellular phenotypes and networks. Patient and public involvement embedded within the Model Systems infrastructure secures the scientific and translational relevance of the activities and helps to link experimental findings in our model systems to clinical symptoms and behavioral dimensions. By integrating animal, cellular, and human data on a multi-systems level with clinically relevant symptoms, the DZPG leverages model systems to accelerate mechanistic discovery and translation in mental health research.
journal: European archives of psychiatry and clinical neuroscience
authors: Safaiyan S, Schmidt MV, Zimprich A, Steiner J, Schulte EC, Böhm C, Spanagel R, Dere E, Zlomuzica A, Fischer-Posovszky P
